m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Install VS Code on Windows, macOS, or a Chromebook.
  • Add the Live Server extension and explain what it does for you.
  • Open the browser Console and run a line of JavaScript in it.
  • Make one course folder that holds every project you build.

By the end of this page you will type 2 + 2 into your browser and it will answer 4. That sounds tiny, but the window you type it into, the Console, is where your code will report every message and every error for the rest of the course. Most people who get stuck in their first JavaScript project are stuck because they never opened it.

You need three free things, and they work as a loop: you write code in an editor, a small local server hands the page to your browser, and the browser runs it and tells you what happened.

#What you need before you start

  • A computer running Windows 10 or 11, macOS 12 or newer, or a Chromebook where Linux can be turned on. Phones and tablets can't run VS Code.
  • Permission to install software. School laptops sometimes block installs. Check now, not the night before a project is due.
  • Google Chrome (or Microsoft Edge, which has the same developer tools). Firefox works too, but the menu names in this course are Chrome's.
  • About 20 minutes on a decent internet connection.

Everything here is free. Download VS Code only from code.visualstudio.com; other sites that offer "free VS Code" downloads sometimes bundle unwanted software.

#Step 1: Install VS Code

VS Code is a code editor from Microsoft. It colors your code so mistakes stand out, suggests names as you type, and runs extensions like Live Server.

Windows

  1. Go to code.visualstudio.com (opens in a new tab) and click Download for Windows. You get the User Installer, which does not need an administrator password.
  2. Open the file from your Downloads folder (it is named something like VSCodeUserSetup-x64-….exe) and accept the license agreement.
  3. On Select Additional Tasks, leave Add to PATH checked. Also tick both Add "Open with Code" action boxes, so you can right-click any folder and open it in VS Code.
  4. If a page asks about the GitHub Copilot CLI, choose Don't add the copilot command. This course doesn't use it, and it needs a paid subscription.
  5. Click Install, then Finish with Launch Visual Studio Code ticked.

macOS

  1. Go to code.visualstudio.com (opens in a new tab) and click Download for macOS. The Universal build runs on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs.
  2. Open the downloaded .dmg file.
  3. Drag Visual Studio Code.app into the Applications folder. Don't run it straight from the disk image or from Downloads, because updates can't install there.
  4. Open VS Code from Applications. If macOS warns that the app was downloaded from the internet and asks if you're sure, click Open.
  5. Optional: Control-click the icon in the Dock and choose Options › Keep in Dock.

Chromebook

  1. Turn on Linux: select the time at the bottom right, then Settings › About ChromeOS › Developers, and next to Linux development environment select Set up. Accept the defaults. This can take 10 minutes or more, and a Terminal window opens when it's done.
  2. In that Terminal, type dpkg --print-architecture and press Enter. It prints amd64 or arm64.
  3. Go to code.visualstudio.com/download (opens in a new tab). Under Linux, choose .deb x64 if you saw amd64, or .deb Arm64 if you saw arm64.
  4. Open the Files app, go to Downloads, double-click the .deb file, and choose Install.
  5. Open the Launcher. VS Code is in the Linux apps folder.

When VS Code opens you'll see a Welcome tab. You can close it. The column of icons on the far left is the Activity Bar; the top icon (two pages) is the Explorer, where your files will appear.

#Step 2: Add the Live Server extension

You could open an HTML file by double-clicking it. The address bar would then start with file://, and the page would not update when you save. Some features you'll use later, like loading data with fetch in Module 6, refuse to work on file:// pages at all. Live Server fixes both problems: it serves your folder at a real web address, http://127.0.0.1:5500, and reloads the browser every time you save a file.

  1. In VS Code, click the Extensions icon in the Activity Bar (four small squares), or press Ctrl+Shift+X (Cmd+Shift+X on a Mac).
  2. Search for Live Server.
  3. Pick the one by Ritwick Dey. It has tens of millions of installs. Click Install.

Nothing visible happens yet. The Go Live button appears in the status bar at the bottom right once you open a folder that contains an HTML file, which you'll do in the next lesson.

#Step 3: Make a course folder

Make one folder for the whole course and one folder inside it for each project. Use lowercase names with dashes instead of spaces, because spaces turn into %20 in web addresses.

  1. In your Documents folder (on a Chromebook, in Linux files inside the Files app), create a folder named js-course.
  2. In VS Code, choose File › Open Folder… and pick js-course.
  3. VS Code asks Do you trust the authors of the files in this folder? It's your own empty folder, so click Yes, I trust the authors.

The folder's name now appears at the top of the Explorer. From here on, always open the folder, not a single file. Live Server serves whatever folder VS Code has open.

#Step 4: Talk to the Console

Open Chrome on any page (a blank new tab works), then open the Console:

Computer Shortcut
Windows or Chromebook Ctrl+Shift+J
Mac Cmd+Option+J
Any, with the mouse Right-click the page, choose Inspect, then click the Console tab

Click next to the > prompt and type each line, pressing Enter after each:

The Console runs JavaScript as soon as you press Enter and shows the result underneath. The last line is a preview of Module 2: a number in quotes is text, and adding text to a number sticks them together instead of doing math.

📝 Note

Chrome may refuse the first time you paste code into the Console and ask you to type allow pasting. That warning exists because scammers trick people into pasting code that steals their accounts. Typing the examples yourself avoids it, and so does never pasting code you don't understand.

#Check that everything works

You're ready for the next lesson when all three are true:

  • VS Code opens with js-course showing in the Explorer.
  • The Extensions view lists Live Server as installed.
  • The Console answers 2 + 2 with 4.

#When something goes wrong

⚠️ Watch out

"Linux development environment" is missing or greyed out on a Chromebook. A school-managed Chromebook usually has Linux turned off by the administrator, and only they can turn it on. Ask your teacher or school IT. Until then you can follow Modules 2–4 with the live previews on these pages and the Console, and edit files with vscode.dev (opens in a new tab) (VS Code in the browser, which can open a folder from your Chromebook). Open your index.html from the Files app to view it in Chrome, and refresh by hand after each save.

⚠️ Watch out

The installer on Windows says you need an administrator. You downloaded the System Installer. Go back to the download page and pick User Installer for your computer (x64 for most laptops, Arm64 for Arm-based ones).

⚠️ Watch out

You can't find the Extensions icon. The Activity Bar can be hidden. Open the Command Palette with Ctrl+Shift+P (Cmd+Shift+P on a Mac), type extensions, and choose Extensions: Install Extensions.

⚠️ Watch out

The Console shows red errors you didn't write. Pages you visit (and some browser extensions) log their own errors. Open the Console on a new blank tab, or click the clear button (a circle with a line through it) at the top of the Console. You only care about errors that point at your own files.

#Further reading

  • VS Code setup overview (opens in a new tab): the official install pages for every operating system, if your setup differs from the steps above.
  • Live Server on the VS Code Marketplace (opens in a new tab): every way to start and stop the server, plus its settings.
  • Chrome DevTools: Console overview (opens in a new tab): what the Console can do beyond what this course uses.

What you'll learn

  • Create index.html and script.js in a project folder and link them with defer.
  • Prove a script is running with console.log and the Console.
  • Recognize the two errors almost everyone hits first: a missing script file and an element that comes back null.
  • Make a button that counts clicks and a second one that resets the count.

Every page you've built with HTML and CSS stays exactly the same no matter how many times you click on it. Here's the first one that doesn't. Click the button a few times:

The previews on these pages keep everything in one file so you can see it at a glance. In your own projects you'll split the HTML and the JavaScript into separate files, which is what real sites do, so that's how you'll build this one.

#Step 1: Make the project folder and the HTML page

  1. Open your js-course folder in VS Code (File › Open Folder…).
  2. In the Explorer, hover over JS-COURSE and click the New Folder icon. Name it 01-counter.
  3. Click 01-counter, then the New File icon. Name it index.html.
  4. In the empty file type ! and press Enter when the Emmet Abbreviation suggestion appears. VS Code fills in a full HTML skeleton.

Edit the skeleton so it matches this:

The new line is the script tag in the head. Its src says which file to load, and defer tells the browser when to run it.

#Step 2: Understand what defer does

A browser reads an HTML file from top to bottom, building each element as it goes. When it meets a plain script tag, it stops, fetches the script, runs it, and only then carries on reading. If that script lives in the head, it runs before the browser has reached the body, so the button doesn't exist yet.

defer changes the deal: fetch the file now, in the background, but wait to run it until the whole page has been read. By then every element is in place.

defer only works on scripts loaded with src. That's why the previews on these pages, which put the code directly inside the script tag, place it at the bottom of the page instead.

#Step 3: Prove the script runs

Create a second file in 01-counter named script.js and give it one line:

Save both files (Ctrl+S, or Cmd+S on a Mac). Now start the server: right-click index.html in the Explorer and choose Open with Live Server. Your browser opens an address like http://127.0.0.1:5500/01-counter/index.html.

Open the Console (Ctrl+Shift+J, or Cmd+Option+J on a Mac). You should see:

The grey script.js:1 on the right means "this came from line 1 of script.js." Click it and DevTools jumps to that line. When something breaks later, that link is how you'll find the line to blame.

console.log prints to the Console, not to the page. Visitors never see it; it's a note to yourself.

#Step 4: See the two classic errors on purpose

Breaking things deliberately, while you know what you changed, is the fastest way to learn what the error messages mean.

Error 1: the browser can't find the file. In index.html, change src="script.js" to src="scripts.js" and save. Live Server reloads the page, the log message disappears, and the Console shows something like:

404 means "no file at that address." The fix is to make src match the file name exactly, including capital letters. Change it back to script.js and save.

Error 2: the element isn't there yet. You'll see this one in Step 5, once the script touches the button.

#Step 5: Make the button count

Replace everything in script.js with this:

Save, switch to the browser, and click Add one a few times. The number on the page goes up, and the Console logs each new value.

Here is what each part does. You'll study all of it properly in Modules 3 and 4, so for now read it like a recipe:

  • document.querySelector("#count") finds the first element that matches a CSS selector, here the one with id="count".
  • let count = 0 makes a variable that is allowed to change. const makes one that isn't.
  • addEventListener("click", () => { … }) says "every time this button is clicked, run the code inside the braces."
  • countDisplay.textContent = count replaces the text inside the span.

Now meet Error 2. In index.html, delete the word defer and save. The counter stops working and the Console shows:

Without defer, the script ran while the browser was still in the head. querySelector("#add") found nothing, which JavaScript represents as null, and null has no addEventListener. Put defer back and save.

⚠️ Watch out

The same null error appears when a selector has a typo, like querySelector("#Add") or querySelector("add") without the #. When you see Cannot read properties of null, check two things: is the selector spelled exactly like the HTML, and does the script have defer?

#Step 6: Add a reset button

Add a second button to index.html, right after the first one:

Then add this to the bottom of script.js:

Save and test: count to 5, press Reset, and the display returns to 0. Notice that Reset has to change two things, the variable and the text on the page. If you only set count = 0, the page keeps showing 5 until the next click. Keeping your data and your page in agreement is a theme that runs through this whole course.

🧪 Try it yourself

Change count + 1 to count + 10 and save. Then add a third button, Subtract one, with its own listener.

#Proof it works

  • The page opens from an http://127.0.0.1:5500/… address, not file://.
  • Clicking Add one raises the number, and Reset puts it back to 0.
  • The Console shows your count is now messages and no red errors.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1You remove defer from a script tag in the head, and the script runs document.querySelector("#add"). What does querySelector give back?

  • It is in the file, but the browser hasn't reached it yet when the script runs.

  • Without defer the script runs as soon as the browser reads its tag, before the button exists.

  • The file loaded fine; a missing file shows a 404 instead.

Show answer

B. Without defer the script runs as soon as the browser reads its tag, before the button exists.

2The Console says GET …/Script.js net::ERR_ABORTED 404 (Not Found), and your file is named script.js. What's the fix?

  • defer changes when the script runs, but the browser can't even find this file.

  • A 404 means nothing exists at that address. Capital letters count on web servers.

  • VS Code isn't the problem; the page is asking for a file name that doesn't exist.

Show answer

B. A 404 means nothing exists at that address. Capital letters count on web servers.

#Further reading

  • MDN: the script element (opens in a new tab): the official reference for src, defer, and async.
  • MDN: What is JavaScript? (opens in a new tab): a friendly overview of how JavaScript fits with HTML and CSS, with more on loading scripts.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Keep every project in its own folder with the same three files.
  • Tell whether a file is saved, and turn on Auto Save.
  • Read a Console error: its type, its message, and the file and line it points to.
  • Use console.log to check what a variable really holds.
  • Follow a short routine when you're stuck, and ask for help in a way that gets answers.

The most common bug in this course won't be in your code. It will be a file you edited but never saved, so the browser keeps running the old version while you stare at the new one. The second most common is a perfectly clear error message sitting in a Console that nobody opened. Both take seconds to fix once you know to look.

#One folder per project

Give every project its own folder inside js-course, and give every project the same three files. When everything looks the same, you always know where to look.

Keep js-course open in VS Code and start each project by right-clicking its index.html and choosing Open with Live Server. The address bar then shows which project you're looking at, for example 127.0.0.1:5500/02-tip-calculator/index.html. If the page looks wrong, glance at that address first: editing one project while viewing another happens to everyone.

#Make sure the browser sees your latest save

VS Code marks an unsaved file with a dot on its tab, and the Explorer shows a number badge for how many files are unsaved. Live Server only reloads when a file is saved, so a dot on a tab means the browser is showing old code.

You have two options:

  • Press Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on a Mac) every time you stop typing.
  • Turn on File › Auto Save. VS Code then saves about a second after you stop typing, and Live Server reloads on its own.

Auto Save is the better choice for this course. If the page ever seems stuck on an old version anyway, do a hard reload in the browser with Ctrl+Shift+R (Cmd+Shift+R on a Mac), which skips the browser's cached copy.

#How to read an error message

When JavaScript hits a line it can't run, it stops and prints an error in red. Every error has the same three parts:

  • The type tells you the category. A ReferenceError means a name doesn't exist. A TypeError means a value was the wrong kind for what you did with it. A SyntaxError means the code isn't valid JavaScript, so none of the file runs.
  • The message is usually more specific than it first looks. "Reading 'textContent'" tells you exactly which property you tried to use on null.
  • The location is a link. Click it to jump to the line.

Each button below runs one line containing a classic mistake. The page catches the error and shows you the real message your browser produces:

Here is what those messages, and a few others you'll meet, usually mean. The wording is Chrome's; other browsers say the same thing differently.

Error message What usually happened First thing to check
totl is not defined You used a name that was never created Spelling, including capital letters
Cannot read properties of null querySelector found nothing The selector, and defer on the script tag
Cannot set properties of null Same as above, while assigning to it Same as above
document.querySelecter is not a function A method name is misspelled Spelling of the method
Assignment to constant variable. You changed a const Use let if it really needs to change
Unexpected end of input A } or ) is missing, so no code in the file runs Matching brackets; VS Code highlights pairs
404 (Not Found) The page asked for a file that isn't there The src path and file name

⚠️ Watch out

Read the first red error, not the last. One early mistake often causes several more below it. Fix the top one, save, and check again before worrying about the rest.

#Use console.log as a flashlight

Errors tell you when JavaScript gives up. Many bugs don't crash, though; they just produce the wrong answer. For those, print the values you're assuming and check whether they're true:

The first line of output is wrong in a puzzling way: 12.53 instead of 37.5. The labelled log doesn't help, because the Console prints 3 the same way whether it's text or a number. The third log gives it away: wrapping variables in { } prints each one with its name, and '3' appears in quotes, so it's text. typeof confirms it. Module 2 explains why 12.5 + "3" sticks the two together.

Two habits make logging much more useful. Label every log, so you know which line printed what. And log just before the line that misbehaves, so you see the values that line actually received.

#A routine for when you're stuck

When you ask a teacher, a classmate, or a forum, include four things: the code as text (not a phone photo of your screen), the exact error message, what you expected to happen, and what you already tried. A question like "my counter shows 5 after I click Reset, here's script.js, there's no error, I checked that count is 0 in the Console" usually gets an answer in minutes. "It doesn't work" gets a list of questions back.

#Comfort, privacy, and safety

  • Make text bigger. In VS Code, View › Appearance › Zoom In (Ctrl+=, or Cmd+= on a Mac). In the browser and DevTools, Ctrl and + (Cmd and +) do the same.
  • Pick a readable theme. VS Code includes high-contrast themes. Open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P, or Cmd+Shift+P on a Mac), run Preferences: Color Theme, and use the arrow keys to preview each one.
  • Keep personal details out of shared code. Before posting code online, remove real names, emails, and passwords. The practice data in this course is invented on purpose.
  • Don't run code you don't understand, whether it came from a forum, a video comment, or an AI tool. Read it line by line first. The Console's allow pasting warning exists because pasted code has stolen real accounts.

Key takeaways

  • One folder per project, each with index.html, style.css, and script.js.
  • A dot on a VS Code tab means the browser is showing old code; Auto Save prevents this.
  • An error's type, message, and file:line link tell you what broke and where. Fix the first red error first.
  • Labelled console.log calls show what your variables hold, which catches the bugs that don't crash.

#Further reading

  • MDN: What went wrong? Troubleshooting JavaScript (opens in a new tab): a beginner walk-through of finding and fixing errors in a small game.
  • MDN: JavaScript error reference (opens in a new tab): look up any error message and get an explanation with examples.
  • Chrome DevTools: Debug JavaScript (opens in a new tab): the step-by-step tutorial behind the video, for when you're ready to try breakpoints.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Tell strings, numbers, and booleans apart, and predict what + does with each.
  • Choose between let and const for a variable.
  • Build readable text with template literals, and round numbers for display.
  • Store a list in an array and a set of named facts in an object.
  • Write a function, in both regular and arrow form, that returns a result.

You read 120 pages on Saturday and 30 on Sunday. Your reading tracker adds them up and proudly reports that you read 12030 pages this weekend. Nothing crashed, and every line ran. JavaScript did exactly what it was told; it just wasn't told what the programmer meant.

The quotes around "120" make it text, and adding a number to text sticks them together. Bugs like this come from data that isn't what you think it is. So before you make pages respond to clicks, you need to describe your data precisely: what type each value is, which values are allowed to change, and how to group values into lists and records.

The run boxes on this page show real output from Node, which runs the same JavaScript language as your browser. To try any example yourself, type it into your browser's Console or into a script.js file.

#Every value has a type, and the type decides what + means

A value is one piece of data: 412, "Dune", true. JavaScript sorts every value into a type. The ones you'll use constantly are numbers, strings (text, in quotes), and booleans (true or false). There's also undefined, which means "no value has been given yet." The typeof operator tells you a value's type:

Arrays and objects both report "object", which is a known oddity. You'll meet both properly below.

Now watch what happens when types mix:

+ has two jobs. If either side is a string, it joins text; otherwise it adds. The other math operators (-, *, /) only do math, so JavaScript quietly converts "120" to a number for them. That inconsistency is why you should convert text to a number yourself, with Number(), the moment it enters your program. If the conversion fails you get NaN ("not a number"), which spreads through every calculation it touches.

⚠️ Watch out

Every value you read from a form field is a string, even from an input type="number". Forgetting this produces the 12030 bug. Convert with Number(input.value) before doing math.

#const for most variables, let for the ones that change

A variable is a name attached to a value. JavaScript gives you two ways to make one. const attaches a name permanently. let lets you attach the name to a new value later:

The let variable updated happily. Reassigning the const stopped the program with TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

Start with const every time, and switch to let only when you know the value has to change, like a running count. Then anyone reading your code can see at a glance which values move. You'll also see var in older tutorials. It's the pre-2015 way of making variables, with confusing rules about where the name is visible, so this course doesn't use it.

#Strings and template literals

Gluing strings with + works, but long messages turn into a mess of quotes and plus signs. Template literals use backticks instead of quotes and let you drop any value into the text with ${…}:

The first two lines print the same sentence, but the second is far easier to read and to get right. The third shows that ${…} can hold a calculation, not just a variable name.

Strings also come with built-in tools. length (no parentheses) counts characters. toUpperCase(), includes(), and trim() are methods, actions you call with parentheses. trim() removes spaces from both ends, which matters as soon as people start typing into your pages and accidentally hit the spacebar.

#Numbers: dividing, rounding, and the decimal surprise

Progress bars, prices, and averages all need division, and division rarely comes out even:

Math.round() gives the nearest whole number. toFixed(1) gives exactly one decimal place, but it returns a string, so use it only for display, as the last step. The last line is the decimal surprise: computers store numbers in binary, and many decimals (like 0.1) can't be stored exactly, so tiny errors creep in. Every language has this. The practical rule is to keep full precision while calculating and round only when you show the result. The next lesson's tip calculator deals with it for money.

#Arrays keep a list in order

An array holds many values in one variable, in order, inside square brackets. Each item has a position number called an index, starting from 0:

The first item is toRead[0], so the last is always at length - 1. Asking for an index that doesn't exist gives undefined, not an error, which is why off-by-one mistakes can hide quietly. push adds to the end, includes checks membership, and join turns the list into one string.

Wait: toRead is a const, yet push changed it. That's allowed. const stops the name from being attached to a different array, but the array itself can still gain and lose items.

#Objects group the facts about one thing

An array is good for "many of the same kind of thing." For the details of one thing, like a single book, you want named slots. An object stores properties as name: value pairs inside curly braces:

A dot reads a property, and assigning to one changes it or adds it. A property that was never set reads as undefined, just like a missing array index.

Real apps combine the two: an array of objects, where each object is one record. Here is the reading tracker's data:

Read readingList[1].title from left to right: take the list, go to index 1 (the second book), then read its title.

#Functions package steps you'll repeat

Working out "percent read" means the same calculation for every book. A function gives those steps a name. Values go in through parameters, and return sends the result back to whoever called it:

percentRead is a function declaration. pagesLeft is an arrow function stored in a const. When an arrow function's body is a single expression with no braces, its value is returned automatically. Both forms do the same job here; you'll see arrow functions a lot in this course, especially for short helpers and for code that runs on a click.

The most common function bug is printing a result instead of returning it:

The 25 appears, so it looks as if the function works. But nothing was returned, so result is undefined, and any code that tries to use it gets nothing.

⚠️ Watch out

console.log shows a value to you; return hands it to the rest of your program. A function that only logs gives back undefined. The same trap appears with arrow functions that use braces: (book) => { book.pages - book.pagesRead } returns undefined because braces need an explicit return.

#Check your data with labelled logs

When a result looks wrong, log the values that went into it, with labels. Wrapping variables in braces prints each one with its name and shows strings in quotes, so a sneaky "120" stands out:

Check your understanding

4 questions

1What does console.log("5" + 2) print?

  • That would need both values to be numbers. "5" is a string.

  • With a string on either side, + joins text, so you get the string "52".

  • NaN comes from a failed conversion to a number, but + never tried to convert here.

Show answer

B. With a string on either side, + joins text, so you get the string "52".

2You need a variable that holds how many pages you've read today, and it goes up every time you log more reading. Which do you use?

  • A const can't be reassigned, so pagesToday = pagesToday + 20 would throw an error.

  • The value has to change, which is exactly what let is for.

  • They differ precisely in whether the name can be reassigned.

Show answer

B. The value has to change, which is exactly what let is for.

3What happens with const shelf = ["Dune"]; shelf.push("Holes");?

  • const blocks reassigning the name, not changing the array's contents.

  • push changes the array the name points to, which const allows.

  • push adds an item to the array; it doesn't join strings.

Show answer

B. push changes the array the name points to, which const allows.

4What does const half = (n) => { n / 2 }; console.log(half(10)); print?

  • It would, without the braces: (n) => n / 2.

  • With braces, an arrow function needs return. This one calculates 5 and throws it away.

  • The code is valid; it just returns nothing.

Show answer

B. With braces, an arrow function needs return. This one calculates 5 and throws it away.

Key takeaways

  • + joins text if either side is a string. Convert input with Number() before doing math.
  • Use const by default and let only for values you'll reassign.
  • Template literals (backticks and ${…}) build readable messages. Round with Math.round or toFixed only for display.
  • Arrays hold ordered lists, starting at index 0. Objects hold named properties. An array of objects describes a list of records.
  • Functions take parameters and return a result; logging is not returning.

#Further reading

  • MDN: Grammar and types (opens in a new tab): the official guide to variables, let and const, and every value type.
  • MDN: Working with objects (opens in a new tab): creating objects, reading and changing properties, and objects inside arrays.
  • MDN: Functions (opens in a new tab): parameters, return values, and arrow functions with many short examples.

m2-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Turn a calculation into a function that takes parameters and returns an object.
  • Find and fix the "text plus number" bug that form input causes.
  • Do money math in whole cents so results come out exact.
  • Format numbers as prices with a template literal.
  • Connect a function to inputs and a button on a real page.

Three friends finish dinner. The bill is $37.40, they want to tip 15%, and someone has to work out what each person pays. Here's the calculator you'll build. Change the numbers and press Calculate:

Most of that code is one function, calculateTip, that knows nothing about web pages. You'll build it first in plain JavaScript, find three bugs that real input causes, and connect it to the page last. Building the logic separately from the page is a habit worth keeping: you can test it in seconds without clicking anything.

#Step 1: Do the math once

Start with plain variables and the obvious formula: the tip is the bill times the percentage, the total is the bill plus the tip, and each person pays a share of the total.

The formula is right, but look at the tip: 5.609999999999999, not 5.61. That's the decimal surprise from the last lesson. And 14.336666666666666 isn't something you can pay. Keep both problems in mind; Step 4 fixes them.

#Step 2: Turn it into a function

Three variables at the top of a file can only describe one dinner. A function with three parameters can describe any dinner. It returns an object so the caller gets all three answers, each with a name:

{ tip, total } is shorthand for { tip: tip, total: total }: when a property has the same name as the variable holding its value, you can write the name once.

Returning an object instead of printing matters. Printing would show the answer to you, but the page needs the numbers themselves so it can display them its own way.

#Step 3: Feed it what a form actually gives you

On the page, the numbers will come from input elements, and input.value is always a string. Here's what happens when the function gets strings:

The tip is still correct, because * and / convert strings to numbers. But bill + tip joined "37.40" and 5.609… into the string "37.405.609999999999999", and dividing that nonsense by 3 gave NaN.

The fix is to convert the moment the text enters your program, so the function always receives numbers:

Converting at the edge, where the data arrives, keeps calculateTip simple: it can trust that it gets numbers and focus on the math.

#Step 4: Count money in whole cents

Now the decimals. Rounding at the end with toFixed(2) hides them, but there's a second, sneakier problem. Split $100.00 three ways and round normally, and everyone pays $33.33. Three times $33.33 is $99.99: the group is a cent short, and the restaurant notices.

Two changes fix both problems:

  1. Work in cents. Whole numbers of cents are exact, so convert the bill to cents first, round the tip to a whole cent, and add integers.
  2. Round each share up with Math.ceil, so the shares always cover the total. Paying a cent extra beats being a cent short.

The tip is now exactly 5.61. For the $100 bill, each share is 33.34, and three of those ($100.02) cover the bill. Math.round(bill * 100) matters too: in JavaScript 19.99 * 100 is 1998.9999999999998, and rounding snaps it back to 1999 cents.

#Step 5: Don't divide by zero people

Someone will clear the People box. An empty input converts to 0, and dividing by zero in JavaScript doesn't crash. It gives Infinity:

Math.max(1, people) picks whichever is larger, so the group size can never drop below 1. Math.floor removes fractions, because 2.7 people can't split a bill. Module 3 shows how to make decisions with if and show a message instead; for a calculator, quietly treating "nobody" as one person is reasonable.

#Step 6: Format the answer for people

The function's job ends at numbers. Turning them into text is a separate, small job, so give it its own function:

In `$${amount.toFixed(2)}` the first $ is a plain dollar sign, and ${ starts the slot for the value. toFixed(2) always shows two decimals, so $43.10 doesn't appear as $43.1.

#Step 7: Put it on a page

Make a folder 02-tip-calculator in js-course with these two files. The HTML gives each input an id so the script can find it, and wraps each input in its label, so clicking the words focuses the box and screen readers announce what the box is for.

The script is the function from Step 6, plus the part that talks to the page:

Open index.html with Live Server and press Calculate. You should see:

The click handler does three things in order: read the inputs and convert them (Step 3), call the function, and write the formatted result into the page with textContent. The aria-live="polite" on the result paragraph asks screen readers to announce the new text when it changes, so someone who can't see the screen still hears the answer.

🧪 Try it yourself

Clear the People box and press Calculate. Then try a bill of 100 with a 0 tip and 3 people, and check that the shares cover the bill.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the click handler call Number(billInput.value) instead of passing billInput.value straight in?

  • Number() only converts text to a number; rounding happens inside calculateTip.

  • That's the Step 3 bug: "37.40" + 5.61 becomes "37.405.61".

  • textContent accepts any text; the problem is in the math, before anything is displayed.

Show answer

B. That's the Step 3 bug: "37.40" + 5.61 becomes "37.405.61".

2Why does the calculator use Math.ceil for each person's share instead of Math.round?

  • Rounding $33.333 down to $33.33 leaves the group a cent short; rounding up never does.

  • Math.round works fine on decimals; it just sometimes rounds down.

  • The tip is calculated before the split and isn't affected.

Show answer

A. Rounding $33.333 down to $33.33 leaves the group a cent short; rounding up never does.

3calculateTip returns an object and never touches the page. What does that buy you?

  • Speed isn't the reason; the function runs in microseconds either way.

  • You tested every step in plain JavaScript without clicking anything, and the page decides the wording.

  • They can; this one just doesn't need to.

Show answer

B. You tested every step in plain JavaScript without clicking anything, and the page decides the wording.

Key takeaways

  • Build the logic as a function that takes parameters and returns an object, then connect it to the page.
  • Convert input text to numbers with Number() where it enters the program.
  • Do money math in whole cents with Math.round, and round shares up with Math.ceil.
  • Guard against impossible input like zero people. Math.max(1, n) sets a floor.
  • Keep formatting separate: formatMoney turns a number into $0.00 text.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add buttons for 15%, 18%, and 20% that fill in the tip box when clicked.
  • Show the tip per person as well as the total per person.
  • Add a "round the total up to a whole dollar" checkbox. (You'll need if from Module 3.)
  • Recalculate as the user types instead of on a click. (That's the input event from Module 4.)

#Further reading

  • MDN: Number() constructor (opens in a new tab): exactly how text converts to numbers, including what gives NaN and 0.
  • MDN: Math.ceil() (opens in a new tab): rounding up, with a comparison to round and floor.
  • MDN: Template literals (opens in a new tab): every feature of backtick strings, including multi-line text.

What you'll learn

  • Predict how +, *, and typeof treat strings and numbers.
  • Write small functions that take parameters and return results.
  • Read, add, and combine data in arrays and objects.
  • Find bugs by logging values and reading what comes back.
  • Make an updated copy of an object without changing the original.

Every exercise here is about the same reading tracker. Write your answer in a script.js file (or straight into the Console), run it, and compare with the sample output before opening the solution. If you're stuck for more than ten minutes, open the hint; if you're still stuck, read the solution, close it, and write it again from memory.

#Warm-up: predict, then check

Write down what each line prints before you look:

Show solution

JavaScript works left to right. In "4" + 2 + 1, the first + joins "4" and 2 into "42", and the second joins "42" and 1. In 4 + 2 + "1", the first + adds two numbers to get 6, and only then meets a string, so the result is "61". * never joins text, so "4" * "2" is 8.

#Exercise 1: Fix the weekend total

This code should report 75 pages, but it says 4530. Fix it without changing the first two lines (pretend they came from a form).

Need a hint?

Both values are strings. Which function turns "45" into the number 45?

Show solution

Number() converts each string before + sees it, so + adds instead of joining.

#Exercise 2: Percent finished

Write a function percentDone(pagesRead, totalPages) that returns the percentage finished as a whole number. Test it with these three calls:

Need a hint?

Divide, multiply by 100, then round. Make sure the function uses return, not console.log.

Show solution

One third is 33.33…%, and Math.round turns it into 33.

#Exercise 3: Describe a book

Write an arrow function describeBook that takes a book object and returns one sentence built with a template literal.

Need a hint?

Start with const describeBook = (book) => followed by a template literal, and put ${book.title} and the other properties inside its backticks.

Show solution

The arrow function has no braces, so the template literal is returned automatically. Splitting it over two lines after => is allowed and keeps long lines readable.

#Exercise 4: Manage the to-read list

Start with const toRead = ["Dune", "Holes"];. Then, in order:

  1. Add "Wonder" and "Hatchet" to the end.
  2. Print how many books are on the list.
  3. Print the last book, using length rather than typing 3.
  4. Print whether "Holes" is on the list.
  5. Print the sentence Next up: Dune. 4 books on the list. using values from the array.
Need a hint?

The last index is always length - 1. The first book is at index 0.

Show solution

Using toRead.length - 1 instead of 3 keeps working when the list grows or shrinks.

#Exercise 5: Two bugs, no errors

This code runs without a single error and prints undefined pages left in undefined. Find both bugs. Add console.log lines to check your guesses before you fix anything.

Need a hint?

Log left on its own: why is it undefined? Then compare the property name in the last line with the one in the object, letter by letter.

Show solution

Bug 1: an arrow function with braces needs return; without it the subtraction is calculated and thrown away. Removing the braces also works: (book) => book.pages - book.pagesRead. Bug 2: titel is a typo, and reading a property that doesn't exist gives undefined instead of an error. Neither bug crashes, which is exactly why logging values matters.

#Exercise 6: Log reading without breaking the original

Write logReading(book, pages) that returns a new book object with pagesRead increased by pages, but never above the book's total. The original object must not change.

Need a hint?

Math.min(a, b) gives the smaller of two numbers, which makes a ceiling. To copy an object and change one property, use spread syntax: { ...book, pagesRead: newValue } copies every property of book, then overwrites pagesRead.

Show solution

...book spreads all of the old properties into the new object, and the pagesRead written after it replaces the copied value. Because wonder itself is never assigned to, it still says 120. Returning updated copies instead of changing the original makes bugs easier to trace later, when several parts of an app share the same data.

#Challenge: How long will it take?

Write readingTime(pages, pagesPerHour) that returns a string like "3 h 20 min", rounded to the nearest minute.

Work it in minutes, the same way the tip calculator worked in cents:

Need a hint?

% gives the remainder after division: 200 % 60 is 20, because 200 minutes is 3 full hours with 20 minutes left over. Math.floor(200 / 60) gives the 3.

Show solution

Rounding once, at the start, to whole minutes keeps both parts as whole numbers. If you round the hours and the minutes separately, you can end up with answers like "3 h 60 min".

Going further: "0 h 30 min" reads oddly. In Module 3 you'll use if to return "30 min" when there are no full hours.

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Compare values with ===, <, &&, and ||, and explain why == causes surprises.
  • Choose between paths with if, else if, and else.
  • Repeat work with for and for...of loops.
  • Transform and narrow arrays with forEach, map, and filter.
  • Find elements with querySelector, change them with textContent and classList, and build new ones with createElement and append.

A school supply store has a button labelled In stock only. Its code filters the product list perfectly: the Console shows exactly the three products that are in stock. Yet all five product cards stay on the page, sold-out backpack included. The data changed, and the page didn't.

That gap is the whole subject of this module. JavaScript never updates the page on its own. Your code has to decide what should be shown (with conditions and loops) and then tell the page to show it (with the DOM). By the end of these notes you'll fix that store.

#Comparisons answer "true or false"

A comparison takes two values and gives back a boolean. These are the ones you'll use:

Operator Means Example that's true
=== is exactly equal to 3 === 3
!== is not exactly equal to "a" !== "b"
< > <= >= less than, greater than, or equal 4.5 < 5
&& both sides are true inStock && price < 5
|| at least one side is true isAdmin || isOwner
! flips true and false !soldOut

JavaScript also has a double-equals, ==, which converts the values to the same type before comparing. That sounds helpful until you see the results:

0 equals "", and 0 equals "0", but "" doesn't equal "0". Nobody can keep those conversion rules in their head, so use === and !== everywhere. If you need to compare a string from an input with a number, convert it yourself first, as in Module 2.

#if, else if, and else choose a path

An if statement runs a block of code only when its condition is true. Add else if for more cases and else for "everything else":

JavaScript checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is true. Order matters: if the >= 25 check came first, a $40 cart would match it and be told to spend more. The last call checks the boundary on purpose. Testing values that sit exactly on a cutoff catches most < versus <= mistakes.

⚠️ Watch out

if (total = 0) is a bug that doesn't crash. A single = assigns 0 to total, and since 0 counts as false, the block never runs, and your total has just been wiped. Comparisons need ===.

📝 Note

An if accepts any value, not only booleans. false, 0, "" (empty string), null, undefined, and NaN count as false; everything else counts as true. So if (name) means "if name isn't empty." Writing if (name !== "") says the same thing more plainly.

#Loops repeat work for every item

A for loop has three parts in its parentheses: where to start, the condition to keep going, and what to do after each pass. A for...of loop is simpler when you only need each item, not its position:

The condition is i < prices.length, not <=. With five prices the indexes are 0 to 4, so <= would run a sixth pass and read prices[5], which is undefined. i++ is shorthand for i = i + 1.

#forEach, map, and filter say what you mean

Most loops over arrays do one of three jobs, and arrays have a method for each. You pass the method a function, and it calls that function once per item:

  • forEach does something with each item and gives back nothing. Use it for actions, like logging or adding an element to the page.
  • map builds a new array of the same length, where each item is whatever your function returned.
  • filter builds a new array containing only the items for which your function returned true.

None of them change the original array, which is why products still has five items after all that filtering. The last line chains them: filter first, then map the survivors to names.

⚠️ Watch out

prices.map((price) => { price * 1.08 }) gives [ undefined, undefined, undefined ]. With braces, the arrow function needs return. Either write (price) => price * 1.08 or (price) => { return price * 1.08; }.

#Find elements and change what they show

When the browser loads your HTML, it builds a tree of objects, one per element, called the DOM (Document Object Model). JavaScript changes the page by changing those objects. document is the root of the tree, and these are the tools you'll use most:

  • document.querySelector("css selector") returns the first matching element, or null if nothing matches.
  • document.querySelectorAll("css selector") returns all matches, as a list you can loop over with forEach.
  • element.textContent reads or replaces the text inside an element.
  • element.classList.add("name"), .remove("name"), and .toggle("name") change the element's classes, so your CSS decides how it looks.

Try both buttons:

toggle adds the class if it's missing and removes it if it's there, so the second button switches the highlight on and off. Changing classes, rather than setting colors directly from JavaScript, keeps all of your styling in CSS where it belongs.

#Build elements from data

To add something new to the page, you make an element with document.createElement("li"), fill it in, and attach it to an element already on the page with append. Put that inside a loop, and you can draw a whole list from an array.

Here's the store with its bug fixed. Every button calls one function, render, and hands it the list to show:

The original bug was a filter whose result went to console.log and nowhere else. The fix is a pattern you'll use in every app from here on:

Three details in render are worth copying:

  • cards.replaceChildren() with nothing in the parentheses removes everything inside the list first. Without it, each click would add five more cards below the old ones.
  • The if inside the loop decides per product whether to add the sold-out class. card.classList.toggle("sold-out", !product.inStock) does the same in one line: with a second argument, toggle adds the class when it's true and removes it when it's false.
  • render(products) at the bottom draws the page once when it loads, before anyone clicks.

⚠️ Watch out

You'll see tutorials build elements with card.innerHTML = …. innerHTML treats the text as HTML, so if any of it came from a user, they can inject markup and scripts into your page. Someone could name a product <img src=x onerror="alert('hacked')"> and that code would run. textContent always shows text as text, so use it for anything that contains data.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A text input holds "16". What does input.value === 16 give?

  • They look the same, but one is a string and one is a number.

  • Convert first: Number(input.value) === 16 is true.

  • The comparison is allowed; it's just never true.

Show answer

B. Convert first: Number(input.value) === 16 is true.

2What does [1, 2, 3].map((n) => { n * 2 }) return?

  • That's the result without braces, or with return n * 2 inside them.

  • The braces make a block, and a block without return gives back undefined for every item.

  • map never returns the original items unless your function returns them.

Show answer

B. The braces make a block, and a block without return gives back undefined for every item.

3A page has five elements with class="card". What does document.querySelector(".card") give you?

  • querySelector always stops at the first match.

  • That's querySelectorAll.

  • null means nothing matched, but five elements do.

Show answer

A. querySelector always stops at the first match.

4Users can type a nickname that your page then displays. Which line shows it safely?

  • innerHTML would run any HTML or script hidden in the nickname.

  • textContent displays exactly the characters typed, and never treats them as code.

  • That adds a CSS class named after the nickname; nothing visible changes.

Show answer

B. textContent displays exactly the characters typed, and never treats them as code.

Key takeaways

  • Use === and !==. == converts types by rules that surprise everyone.
  • if / else if / else runs the first block whose condition is true, so order your checks from most to least specific.
  • forEach performs an action per item, map transforms every item, and filter keeps the items that pass a test. None change the original array.
  • querySelector finds an element, textContent and classList change it, and createElement plus append add new ones.
  • Draw the page from the data with a render function that clears and rebuilds, and call it whenever the data or the filter changes.

#Further reading

  • MDN: Making decisions in your code (opens in a new tab): if, else, comparison and logical operators, with interactive examples.
  • MDN: Manipulating documents (opens in a new tab): a hands-on tour of the DOM tree, selecting elements, and creating new ones.
  • MDN: Equality comparisons and sameness (opens in a new tab): the full story of == versus ===, if you want to see why the rules are so strange.

What you'll learn

  • Store an app's data in an array of objects and draw the page from it.
  • Write a render function that clears a list and rebuilds it with createElement and append.
  • Use if / else if / else to choose a status message.
  • Use filter to count tasks and to remove finished ones.
  • Keep data and page in agreement every time something changes.

Here's the finished list. Tick a task, add a new one, try adding an empty one, then press Clear completed:

The important idea is invisible: the page is never edited by hand. The tasks live in an array called todos, and a function called render draws the list from that array. When something changes, the code changes the array first and then redraws. You'll build it in that order.

#Step 1: Write the HTML and CSS

Create 03-todo-list inside js-course, with index.html, style.css, and script.js. The HTML has an empty ul; JavaScript will fill it.

The .done class is the only styling JavaScript will touch. It adds and removes the class, and the CSS decides what "done" looks like.

#Step 2: Describe the tasks as data

Each task has two facts: its text, and whether it's done. That's an object, and the list is an array of them. Start script.js with:

Open the page with Live Server and look in the Console. console.table draws an array of objects as a table, which is easier to read than nested braces. Remove that line once you've seen it.

todos uses let, not const, because Step 7 replaces the whole array with a filtered copy.

#Step 3: Draw one task

Write a function that takes one task object and returns a finished li. Each task gets a real checkbox inside a label, so clicking the text ticks the box, and keyboard users can reach every task with Tab and tick it with Space.

label.append(checkbox, ` ${todo.text}`) adds two things at once: the checkbox element, then the text. When you pass append a string, it becomes plain text on the page, never HTML, so it's as safe as textContent. classList.toggle("done", todo.done) with a second argument adds the class when todo.done is true and removes it when it's false.

#Step 4: Draw the whole list

render empties the list and draws every task again:

Save and check the browser: three tasks appear, and the first is crossed out. Then try this experiment. Temporarily delete the list.replaceChildren(); line and add a second render(); call at the bottom. Every task appears twice, because render added a fresh set below the old one. Put the line back and remove the extra call. Clearing first is what makes it safe to call render as often as you like.

#Step 5: Say how many are left

The summary line needs a decision with three outcomes, which is what if / else if / else is for:

Add renderSummary(); as the last line inside render. filter((todo) => !todo.done) keeps the unfinished tasks, and .length counts them. The empty-list check comes first: with zero tasks, left is also 0, so checking left === 0 first would cheerfully announce "All done!" for a list that never had anything on it.

#Step 6: Tick a task off

When a checkbox changes, update the data, then update the page. Add this inside createItem, just before label.append(…):

todo here is the very object stored in the array, so todo.done = … changes the data itself. Notice that this handler updates just one item and the summary instead of calling render. Redrawing the whole list would replace the checkbox you just pressed with a brand-new one, and a keyboard user's focus would vanish from the list. Everywhere else, calling render is the simple choice.

#Step 7: Add tasks and clear finished ones

Two buttons left. Add reads the input, refuses blank tasks, pushes a new object, and redraws. Clear completed replaces the array with a filtered copy and redraws.

trim() matters: without it, a task made of three spaces would pass the === "" check. return inside the if ends the function early, so nothing below it runs for a blank task. After adding, input.focus() puts the cursor back in the box, ready for the next task.

Clear completed is why todos is a let. filter doesn't delete anything from the old array; it builds a new one with only the unfinished tasks, and todos = swaps it in.

#The finished script

Here is all of script.js in order. It's the same code as the preview at the top of this page.

Test it the way a user would: tick and untick every task with the mouse, then again using only Tab and Space. Add a task, try adding a blank one, clear completed, then clear everything and check that the summary says the list is empty.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why is todos declared with let instead of const?

  • push works fine on a const array; it changes the contents, not the name.

  • filter returns a new array, and todos = … reassigns the name, which const forbids.

  • Changing a property of an object inside the array is allowed even with const.

Show answer

B. filter returns a new array, and todos = … reassigns the name, which const forbids.

2What would happen if render didn't start with list.replaceChildren()?

  • It would look the same only the very first time.

  • append adds to whatever is already in the list, so old items would pile up.

  • Appending more items is perfectly legal, which is why this bug is easy to miss.

Show answer

B. append adds to whatever is already in the list, so old items would pile up.

3In renderSummary, why is todos.length === 0 checked before left === 0?

  • The first true condition wins, so the more specific case has to come first.

  • filter on an empty array just returns another empty array.

  • It does: only the first block whose condition is true runs.

Show answer

A. The first true condition wins, so the more specific case has to come first.

Key takeaways

  • Keep the app's data in one place (here an array of objects) and draw the page from it.
  • A render function clears with replaceChildren() and rebuilds with createElement and append, so it's safe to call any time.
  • Change the data first, then update the page. Never let them drift apart.
  • filter counts things (.length) and removes things (by building a new array).
  • Real checkboxes in labels make the list usable with a keyboard and a screen reader.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a Delete button to each task that removes just that one. (Hint: filter out the object that matches.)
  • Show tabs for All, Active, and Done that change which tasks render draws.
  • Let Enter in the text box add a task. You'll do this properly with a form in Module 4.
  • Keep the list when the page reloads. That's localStorage, coming in Module 5.

  • MDN: Document.createElement() (opens in a new tab): creating elements, with examples of building and attaching them.
  • MDN: Element.replaceChildren() (opens in a new tab): clearing an element or swapping its contents in one call.
  • MDN: Element.classList (opens in a new tab): add, remove, toggle with its second argument, and contains.

What you'll learn

  • Write if / else if chains that handle every case, including bad input.
  • Use loops and array methods to count, average, and pick items.
  • Draw lists and tables from arrays with createElement, textContent, and classList.
  • Find bugs that don't throw errors by checking what the page shows.

The first three exercises are plain JavaScript; run them in the Console or a script.js file and compare with the sample output. Exercises 4 to 6 and the challenge change a page, so build them in a project folder with Live Server. Each solution includes a live preview you can click.

#Warm-up: which branch runs?

For each call, predict which message is printed:

Show solution

"very hot" can never be returned: anything above 30 is caught by the first check. 20 isn't greater than 20, so it falls through to "cool". And "25" gives "warm" because > converts the string to a number, which works here but is the kind of luck you shouldn't depend on.

#Exercise 1: Letter grades

Write letterGrade(score) that returns "A" for 90 and up, "B" for 80–89, "C" for 70–79, "D" for 60–69, and "F" below 60. Scores below 0 or above 100 should return "Invalid score".

Need a hint?

Check for invalid scores first, using ||. Then go from the highest grade down, so each else if only needs a lower bound.

Show solution

Because the checks run in order, reaching score >= 80 already means the score is below 90, so there's no need to write score >= 80 && score < 90. Testing 90 exactly checks the boundary.

#Exercise 2: Class statistics with a loop

Given const scores = [88, 92, 67, 74, 59, 100];, use one for...of loop to work out the number of passing scores (70 or more), the average, and the highest score. Don't use Math.max.

Need a hint?

Before the loop, make three variables with let: a pass counter at 0, a running total at 0, and highest set to the first score. Inside the loop, update each one. Divide the total by scores.length after the loop.

Show solution

Starting highest at the first score, not at 0, means the code still works if every score is negative (say, temperatures in winter).

#Exercise 3: A shopping shortlist

From this list, make an array of labels for products that are in stock and cost under $10, formatted like "Notebook - $4.50". Use filter and map, not a loop.

Need a hint?

Filter first (both conditions joined with &&), then map the survivors to strings. price.toFixed(2) gives two decimal places.

Show solution

Putting each method on its own line, starting with a dot, makes a chain read like a recipe: take the products, keep these, turn them into that.

#Exercise 4: Flag low stock

Start with this page. Write the script that draws one li per item, with text like Pencils: 3 left, and adds the class low to any item with fewer than 5 left.

Need a hint?

Find the ul once with querySelector. Then supplies.forEach: inside, createElement("li"), set its textContent, use classList.toggle("low", item.count < 5), and append it.

Show solution

toggle with a second argument replaces a whole if statement: it adds low when the condition is true and leaves it off when it's false.

#Exercise 5: Draw a scoreboard table

Build a table body from an array of players: one row per player, with a name cell and a points cell. Highlight the leader's row with the class leader. If two players tie for first, highlight both.

Need a hint?

Do it in two passes. First loop to find the top score. Then forEach player: make a tr, make two td elements, append both to the row, and toggle leader when player.points === topScore. (Don't name the variable top: browsers already use that name for the top-level window.)

Show solution

Finding the top score before drawing anything is what makes ties work. Comparing each player with the one before it would only ever mark a single leader.

#Exercise 6: The button that lies

Each click on Show results should list every score and say how many passed. Instead, every click adds another copy of the list, and it claims all six scores passed. There are no errors in the Console. Find both bugs.

Need a hint?

Bug 1: what's already inside results the second time the button is clicked? Bug 2: read the if condition very slowly. => and >= are different operators.

Show solution

Bug 1: nothing cleared the list, so each click appended six more items; results.replaceChildren() at the start fixes it. Bug 2: score => 70 isn't a comparison at all. It's an arrow function (take score, return 70), and a function counts as true, so every score "passed." Click the fixed button twice and the list stays at six, with 4 of 6 passing.

#Challenge: A filter panel with an empty state

Build a product panel with buttons for All, Paper, Writing, Bags, and Art. Clicking a button shows only that category's products and marks that button as active. Art has no products, so it should show No products in this category yet. instead of an empty space.

Use this data, and give each button a data-category attribute (all, paper, writing, bags, art):

Need a hint?

Store the current choice in one variable, let active = "all";. Every button gets the same listener: set active from button.dataset.category (an attribute written data-category in HTML is read as dataset.category in JavaScript), then call render. Inside render, pick the list with an if, check its length for the empty state, and loop over all the buttons to toggle an active class. For screen readers, also set aria-pressed to "true" or "false".

Show solution

Everything flows through one variable, active, and one function, render. The buttons never change the page directly; they only change active and ask for a redraw, so the cards and the highlighted button can't disagree. aria-pressed tells screen readers which filter is on, since they can't see the dark background.

m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Attach a listener with addEventListener and pass it a function without calling it.
  • Read event.type, event.target, and event.key from the event object.
  • Choose between the input, change, keydown, and submit events.
  • Stop a form from reloading the page with event.preventDefault().
  • Write validation messages that say what's wrong and how to fix it, and connect them to their fields for screen readers.
  • Handle clicks for a whole list with one delegated listener and closest.

Here's a sign-up form that many beginners ship. You type a username, leave the email blank by accident, and press Sign up. The page flashes and reloads. Everything you typed is gone, the address bar now ends in ?username=sam&email=, and nothing tells you what went wrong. Someone using only a keyboard and a screen reader gets even less: no message, and no idea which field to fix.

Each of those problems is fixed by handling events, the browser's announcements that something just happened. You've used click as a recipe; now you'll see how events really work.

#"When this happens, run that": addEventListener

element.addEventListener(type, listener) tells the browser: whenever an event of this type happens on this element, call this function. The function is called a listener or handler. One named function can serve several elements:

Look at how handleClick is passed: by name, with no parentheses. You're handing the browser the function so it can call it later, once per click.

⚠️ Watch out

button.addEventListener("click", handleClick()) is a silent bug. The parentheses call handleClick immediately, once, while the page loads, and then pass its return value (undefined) as the listener. There's no error, but clicking does nothing. Pass the function itself: handleClick or () => handleClick().

#The event object tells you what happened

When the browser calls your listener, it passes one argument: an event object describing what happened. Every event has type (like "click") and target, the element the event happened on. That's how handleClick above knows which button was pressed. Other events add their own details. Keyboard events have key, the key that was pressed:

Try Shift, an arrow key, and Backspace. Each has a name: "Shift", "ArrowLeft", "Backspace". Comparing event.key with one of those names is how keyboard shortcuts work.

These are the events you'll use most:

Event Fires when Good for
click an element is clicked, or a focused button is activated with Enter or Space buttons
input the value of a field changes, on every keystroke, paste, or delete live counters, search as you type
change a value is committed: a checkbox is ticked, a menu choice is picked, or a text field is left after editing checkboxes, menus
keydown a key is pressed down keyboard shortcuts
focusout an element loses focus, for example when someone tabs away checking a field when the user leaves it
submit a form is sent, by its button or by pressing Enter in a field forms

#React while someone types: the input event

input fires after every change to a field's value, however it happened: typing, pasting, dictation, or autofill. That makes it the right event for anything that should update live:

Why not keydown? It fires before the new character lands in the box, so bio.value would always be one character behind, and it doesn't fire at all when someone pastes with the mouse. And change only fires when the user leaves a text field, which is too late for a live counter. aria-describedby links the counter to the textarea, so a screen reader reads "0 / 80 characters" along with the field's label.

#Forms: listen for submit, then call preventDefault

A form element has a built-in behavior from the days before JavaScript: when it's submitted, the browser sends the field values to the address in its action attribute and loads the reply as a new page. With no action, it reloads the current page with the values in the address bar. That's the vanishing form from the opening.

To handle a form yourself, listen for submit on the form and call event.preventDefault(), which cancels the browser's built-in behavior for that event. Run this one in your own project with Live Server. Submitting a form makes the browser load a new page, which the embedded previews on this site don't allow.

Type a name and press Enter in either field: the message appears and the page stays put. Now comment out the preventDefault line, save, and try again. The message flashes for an instant, then the page reloads and the address bar shows:

Listen on the form, not on the button's click: pressing Enter in any field also submits the form, and submit catches both routes. (A button inside a form is a submit button unless it has type="button".)

#Validation messages people can actually use

HTML can already check simple rules. Add required, type="email", or minlength="8" to an input, and the browser refuses to submit the form and shows a small bubble until the rule passes. That's a good start and works even if your JavaScript fails. But the bubbles look different in every browser, vanish after a few seconds, and only show one problem at a time. Most real sites add novalidate to the form, which switches the bubbles off, and display their own messages next to each field.

A useful message says what's wrong and how to fix it:

Vague Useful
Invalid input Include an @ in your email, like sam@school.org.
Error in password Use at least 8 characters, including a number.
Field required Enter a username.

Three details make messages work for everyone:

  • Put the message in its own element right after the field, and link them with aria-describedby="email-error" on the input. Screen readers then read the message when the field gets focus.
  • Mark a failing field with aria-invalid="true", and remove it once the field is fixed.
  • Don't rely on red alone. The text of the message has to carry the meaning, because some people can't tell red from green.

Timing matters too. Nobody likes being told off halfway through typing their email. A polite pattern is: check a field when the user leaves it (if they typed something), then re-check on every input while an error is showing, so it disappears the moment it's fixed. Try it: type sam and press Tab, then finish the address.

emailProblem returns a message, or an empty string when all is well. Keeping the rule in its own function means you can test it with plain values and reuse it on submit. Its empty-field message never shows here, because leaving an empty field isn't checked; that one waits for Sign up. The CSS selector input[aria-invalid="true"] styles exactly the fields your code has marked.

📝 Note

Browser checks and JavaScript checks only help honest users fill in the form correctly. Anyone can switch off JavaScript or send data straight to a server, so a real site always checks everything again on the server before trusting it.

#One listener for a whole list: event delegation

When you click a button inside an li inside a ul, the click event doesn't stop at the button. It bubbles up: first the button's listeners run, then the li's, then the ul's, and so on up to document.

So instead of attaching a listener to every Remove button, attach one to the list and ask which button was clicked. This is event delegation. It has a big advantage: buttons created later, by a render call, work automatically, because the listener lives on the list, which never gets replaced.

Add a few items, then remove them. Every new Remove button works, yet there's only one click listener for the whole list. Here's how it finds its way:

  • event.target is the exact element clicked. If you clicked the list's empty space or the item text, it's not a button.
  • event.target.closest("button") walks up from the target and returns the nearest button, or null. That also handles buttons with an icon or a span inside them, where target would be the inner element. If there's no button, the listener returns early.
  • remove.dataset.id = item.id stored the item's id on the button as a data-id attribute. Attributes are always text, so it comes back out as a string and needs Number() before comparing with !==.
  • The aria-label gives each button a full name like "Remove Glue sticks", so a screen reader user hears which item each button removes instead of "Remove, Remove, Remove."

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A page runs saveButton.addEventListener("click", save());. What happens?

  • That needs save without parentheses, so the browser can call it later.

  • The parentheses call save immediately and register its return value, undefined, as the listener.

  • Registering undefined is allowed, so there's no error at all, which is why this bug is easy to miss.

Show answer

B. The parentheses call save immediately and register its return value, undefined, as the listener.

2Which event should drive a "characters remaining" counter under a text box?

  • It fires after every change to the value, including pastes, so the count is always current.

  • For text fields, change waits until the user leaves the field.

  • It fires before the new character is added, and not at all for a mouse paste.

Show answer

A. It fires after every change to the value, including pastes, so the count is always current.

3Why listen for submit on the form instead of click on its Sign up button?

  • They do work, but they miss one way of submitting.

  • One listener on the form handles the button and the Enter key.

  • It's exactly the event that needs preventDefault, to stop the page reload.

Show answer

B. One listener on the form handles the button and the Enter key.

4A ul has a delegated click listener. Later, render() adds a new li with its own Remove button. Does clicking that button trigger the listener?

  • Delegation works for elements created at any time, as long as they're inside the element with the listener.

  • That's true for listeners attached to each button, not for one attached to the parent.

  • Attaching it again would make it run twice per click.

Show answer

A. Delegation works for elements created at any time, as long as they're inside the element with the listener.

Key takeaways

  • addEventListener(type, handler) takes the function itself; handler() with parentheses calls it too early.
  • The event object tells you what happened: type, target, and extras like key.
  • Use input for live updates, change for committed choices, keydown for shortcuts, and submit on the form for forms.
  • event.preventDefault() cancels the browser's built-in behavior, such as reloading the page when a form submits.
  • Good validation messages say how to fix the problem, sit next to their field, and are linked with aria-describedby and aria-invalid.
  • One listener on a parent plus event.target.closest(…) handles every child, including ones added later.

#Further reading

  • MDN: Introduction to events (opens in a new tab): listeners, event objects, and preventDefault, with live examples.
  • MDN: Event bubbling (opens in a new tab): exactly how events travel through the page, and how delegation uses it.
  • MDN: Client-side form validation (opens in a new tab): HTML validation attributes, the built-in messages, and writing your own.
