What you'll learn

  • Write validation rules as one plain function that you can test without a page.
  • Show each error next to its field, linked with aria-describedby and aria-invalid.
  • Handle submit with preventDefault, then either focus the first problem or show success.
  • Re-check fields as people type and when they leave a field, without nagging.
  • Test a form with only a keyboard.

The school coding club needs a sign-up form. It has five fields: a username, an email, a password, the password again, and a checkbox to agree to the club rules. The form you'll build behaves like this when someone presses Sign up:

It also re-checks a field when the user leaves it, and clears a message the moment the problem is fixed. All of it runs in your own project, because the final step handles a real form submission.

#Step 1: Write the form

Create 04-signup in js-course with index.html, style.css, and script.js. Every input gets a visible label, an empty paragraph waiting for its error message, and an aria-describedby that points at that paragraph (and at the hint text, when there is one).

Three attributes are doing quiet work. novalidate on the form turns off the browser's own pop-up bubbles, since you'll show better messages yourself. autocomplete lets password managers and browsers fill fields correctly; new-password tells them this is a new account, so they can suggest a strong password. role="status" on the last paragraph makes screen readers announce the welcome message when it appears.

#Step 2: Write the rules as one function

The rules don't need a page at all: given five values, decide what's wrong with them. Write them as a function that takes an object of values and returns an object of error messages, with one property per problem field. An empty object means everything passed. Because it's plain JavaScript, you can test it right here:

Each test starts from good, a set of values that should pass, and changes one or two things with spread syntax. The first result is {}, so a valid form really is accepted, and each later test shows exactly the message you expected. That's five tests in a fraction of a second, with no clicking. Writing the tests first, before touching the page, catches most mistakes in the rules.

A few decisions are worth noticing:

  • Each field's checks are an if / else if chain, so a field gets one message at a time, the most basic problem first. Telling someone their empty username is both missing and too short isn't helpful.
  • hasDigit loops over a string with for...of, which visits one character at a time. char >= "0" && char <= "9" works because digits sit next to each other in character order.
  • looksLikeEmail only catches obvious typos. No simple rule can prove an address is real; real sites confirm by sending an email to it.

Copy the three functions (without the test lines) into script.js.

⚠️ Watch out

Never put your own password in test data or source code, even as an example. Code gets shared, uploaded, and screenshotted. Use obviously made-up values like pizza2026.

#Step 3: Read the values and show messages

Next, the code that connects the rules to the page. Add this below the rules in script.js:

readValues trims the username and email, because a stray space there is always a mistake. It doesn't trim passwords: a space might be a deliberate part of one, and silently changing a password means the person can't log in later. For the checkbox, .checked gives true or false.

Two new pieces of syntax appear. `#${field}` builds a selector from a variable, so one function can handle every field. And errors[field] reads the property whose name is stored in field: when field is "email", it's the same as errors.email. Fields with no problem aren't in the object, so errors[field] is undefined, and || "" swaps that for an empty string, which clears the message.

#Step 4: Handle the submit

Now the moment from the diagram. Add the submit listener:

Start Live Server and press Sign up with everything empty. You should see:

fields.filter((field) => errors[field]) keeps the names of fields that have a message, in the order they appear on the page, so problems[0] is the problem nearest the top. Moving focus there does two jobs. Sighted users see where to start. Screen reader users hear the field's label followed by its hint and error message, because of aria-describedby, instead of being left on a button with no idea what went wrong.

On success, form.reset() empties every field, and the welcome message appears in the role="status" paragraph. This form doesn't send the data anywhere; in a real app, this is where you'd send it to a server, which you'll learn to do with fetch in Module 6.

#Step 5: Check fields as people go

Waiting for Sign up works, but it's nicer to hear about a typo while you're still near the field. Add two more listeners. Both go on the form, using delegation: focusout and input events from every field bubble up to it.

The focusout listener checks the field the user just left, but skips empty fields and the checkbox: tabbing past something isn't a mistake yet. The input listener re-checks only fields that are already showing a message, so errors disappear the moment they're fixed, but new ones never pop up mid-word. It re-checks all of them, not just the field being typed in, because fixing the password can also fix the "doesn't match" message under Confirm password.

Here's that behavior on its own. The preview leaves out the Sign up button and the submit listener, which need your Live Server project. Type sam lee as a username and press Tab, then replace the space with an underscore. Try a password without a number, too.

#Step 6: Test it like a user

Run through this list in your Live Server project. Do the first three with your mouse untouched.

  1. Press Tab from the top of the page. Focus should visit every field and the checkbox in order, then Sign up.
  2. With the cursor in any text box, press Enter on an empty form. Every message appears, and the cursor jumps to Username.
  3. Tick the checkbox with Space, fill everything in correctly, and press Enter. The welcome message appears and the form clears.
  4. Type a password, then a different confirmation, and leave the field. Fix the first password to match; the confirm message should disappear.
  5. Type sam_lee with spaces around it. It should be accepted, because the spaces are trimmed.

If you have time, turn on your computer's screen reader (Narrator on Windows with Windows logo key+Ctrl+Enter, VoiceOver on a Mac with Cmd+F5, ChromeVox on a Chromebook with Ctrl+Alt+Z) and submit the empty form. You should hear the username label, its hint, and its error message.

#The finished script

All of script.js, in order: the rules from Step 2, then Steps 3, 4, and 5.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why are the rules in validateSignup(values) instead of inside the submit listener?

  • Listeners can contain any code at all.

  • Step 2 tested every rule in plain JavaScript, and three different listeners call the same function.

  • Speed isn't the point; the checks take microseconds either way.

Show answer

B. Step 2 tested every rule in plain JavaScript, and three different listeners call the same function.

2After a failed submit, why does the code call focus() on the first field with a problem?

  • aria-describedby makes the error part of what's announced when that field gets focus.

  • Focus doesn't change the message; fixing the value does.

  • The messages show either way; focus is about where the user is, not what's visible.

Show answer

A. aria-describedby makes the error part of what's announced when that field gets focus.

3readValues trims the email but not the password. Why?

  • They can, and some people use passphrases with spaces in them.

  • Trimming is safe for an email, where a stray space is always a typo, but not for a secret the user chose.

  • trim() is a string method and works on any text.

Show answer

B. Trimming is safe for an email, where a stray space is always a typo, but not for a secret the user chose.

Key takeaways

  • Put validation rules in one plain function that returns an object of messages, and test it with sample values before building the page.
  • Show one message per field, the most basic problem first, right beside the field it describes.
  • aria-describedby, aria-invalid, and moving focus to the first problem make errors usable without a mouse or a screen.
  • Listen for submit on the form and call preventDefault. Check on focusout only when something was typed, and re-check on input only where a message is already showing.
  • Browser-side checks help people fill in a form; a server must still check everything before trusting it.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a Show password checkbox that switches both password fields between type="password" and type="text".
  • Show a strength meter under the password that updates on every input event.
  • Add an age field that only accepts whole numbers between 13 and 18, with a clear message for each kind of mistake.
  • Check whether a username is taken. That needs a server to ask, which is what fetch is for in Module 6.

#Further reading

  • W3C WAI: User notifications (opens in a new tab): the accessibility standards group's guide to success and error messages in forms, with code.
  • MDN: the submit event (opens in a new tab): when submit fires, and what event.submitter tells you about the button used.
  • MDN: aria-describedby (opens in a new tab): how linking a field to its hint and error changes what screen readers announce.

m4-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Pick the right event for a job and read what you need from the event object.
  • React to typing with input and to keys with keydown.
  • Write a validation function that returns a helpful message, and test it with plain values.
  • Handle a list of buttons with one delegated listener and data- attributes.
  • Turn a click-only widget into a form that works with the Enter key.

Exercises 1–3, 5, and 6 change a page: build each in a project folder with Live Server, then compare with the solution's live preview. Exercise 4 is plain JavaScript. The challenge submits a form, so it can only run in your own project. For the keyboard exercise, click inside a preview first so it receives your key presses.

#Warm-up: which event?

Name the event you'd listen for in each case, and the element you'd attach it to:

  1. A "characters left" counter under a comment box.
  2. A newsletter form that should work with the Enter key.
  3. A dropdown menu where picking a size updates the price.
  4. Pressing Escape closes a pop-up anywhere on the page.
  5. Twenty "Add to cart" buttons in a product grid that's redrawn whenever the filter changes.
Show solution
  1. input on the textarea: it fires after every change, including pastes.
  2. submit on the form, with event.preventDefault(): it catches both the button and Enter.
  3. change on the select: it fires once a choice is made.
  4. keydown on document, checking event.key === "Escape": the key press can happen while focus is anywhere.
  5. One click listener on the grid's container, using event.target.closest("button"): the buttons are replaced on every redraw, but the container isn't.

#Exercise 1: A theme switch

Make a button that switches a page between light and dark. Each click toggles a dark class on the body, changes the button's text between Dark mode and Light mode, and sets aria-pressed to "true" or "false".

Need a hint?

classList.toggle("dark") returns true if it just added the class and false if it removed it. Store that in a variable and use it for both the text and aria-pressed. Remember that setAttribute needs a string: String(isDark).

Show solution

isDark ? "Light mode" : "Dark mode" is the conditional operator: a compact if/else that produces a value. It reads "if isDark, then this, otherwise that." An if/else that sets textContent in each branch works just as well.

#Exercise 2: Keyboard shortcuts for a search box

Pressing / anywhere on the page should jump into the search box, like it does on many big websites. Pressing Escape while in the box should clear it and leave the box. Typing / inside the box must still type a slash.

Need a hint?

Listen for keydown on document. document.activeElement is the element that currently has focus. For /, only act when focus is not already in the box, and call event.preventDefault() so the slash isn't typed into it. For Escape, set the value to "" and call search.blur().

Show solution

preventDefault on a keydown stops the key's normal effect, which here would be typing a slash into the box that just got focus. Checking inBox first is what keeps the slash typeable when you're already searching.

#Exercise 3: A live password checklist

Under a password box, show three rules: at least 8 characters, contains a number, and contains a capital letter. On every keystroke, each rule should say Done: or Not yet: in front of it and turn green when met. Store the rules as an array of objects, each with a label and a test function, and draw the list from that array.

Need a hint?

A property can hold a function: { label: "contains a number", test: (pw) => … }. To check for a capital letter, loop over the characters and compare each with char >= "A" && char <= "Z". Use some: [...pw].some((char) => char >= "0" && char <= "9") turns the string into an array of characters and asks whether any one passes.

Show solution

Adding a fourth rule is one new line in the array; nothing else changes. That's the payoff of keeping rules as data. The words Done and Not yet matter as much as the color: they carry the meaning for anyone who can't see green.

#Exercise 4: Validate an age

Write ageProblem(text) for a club open to ages 13 to 18. It takes the raw text from an input and returns a message, or "" if the age is fine:

JSON.stringify in the tests just wraps each result in quotes, so an empty string is visible as "".

Need a hint?

Trim first, then check for empty. Number("fifteen") is NaN, and Number.isInteger(value) is false for both NaN and 14.5, so one check handles both. Only then compare with 13 and 18.

Show solution

Each if returns as soon as it finds a problem, so the checks run from most basic to most specific, and the age comparisons never see NaN. These separate if statements do the same job as an else if chain, because return stops the function.

#Exercise 5: A chore list with one listener

Draw a list of chores from an array. Each chore has a Done button and a Delete button. Use a single click listener on the ul. Give every button a data-action ("done" or "delete") and a data-id, and use them to decide what to change in the array before redrawing.

Need a hint?

In the listener: const button = event.target.closest("button"), return early if it's null, then read button.dataset.action and Number(button.dataset.id). For Done, find the chore with chores.find((chore) => chore.id === id) and flip its done. For Delete, filter it out.

Show solution

find returns the first item that passes the test (or undefined if none does), which is exactly what you want when ids are unique. A data-action attribute lets one listener tell many kinds of button apart. Redrawing here does move keyboard focus off the button, which is fine for a short list; the to-do build showed how to avoid it when it matters.

#Exercise 6: Search as you type

Show a list of eight school clubs and a search box above it. As the user types, show only clubs whose names contain the search text, ignoring capital letters. When nothing matches, show No clubs match "chess". (with whatever was typed) instead of an empty list. Show the number of matches, too.

Need a hint?

Use the input event. Lowercase both sides before comparing: club.toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase()). Then reuse the render pattern from Module 3: clear the list, draw the matches, and check length for the empty message.

Show solution

An empty search box gives the query "", and every string includes the empty string, so the full list shows when the page loads. aria-live="polite" on the count means screen reader users hear "3 of 8 clubs" as they type, without the reader interrupting itself on every keystroke. Notice the message uses textContent, so typing HTML into the box just displays it as text.

#Challenge: Turn the to-do list into a real form

The to-do list from Module 3 only adds a task when you click Add. Upgrade it:

  1. Wrap the input and button in a form, so Enter adds a task. Handle submit and call preventDefault.
  2. Reject an empty task, and a task that's already on the list (ignoring capital letters), with a message under the input. Link the message with aria-describedby, set aria-invalid, and clear both when a task is added.
  3. Replace the per-checkbox listeners with one change listener on the ul, and add a Delete button to each task, handled by one click listener on the ul.

Since it submits a form, build and test this in your own project with Live Server.

Need a hint?

Give each task an id so the delegated listeners can find it: store nextId and increase it after each add. Put data-id on both the checkbox and the Delete button. In the change listener, event.target is the checkbox, so event.target.checked is its new state. For the duplicate check, todos.some((todo) => todo.text.toLowerCase() === text.toLowerCase()) is true if any task matches.

Show solution

The change listener updates one item in place instead of calling render, for the same reason as in the original build: redrawing would destroy the checkbox the user is focused on. The submit listener's two early returns mean a task is only added once it passes every check. Because focus returns to the input after each add, someone can type a task, press Enter, and type the next without touching the mouse. Test exactly that, then try adding finish MATH worksheet to see the duplicate message.

What you'll learn

  • Predict the order in which code runs when setTimeout is involved.
  • Start and stop a repeating timer with setInterval and clearInterval, without starting two by accident.
  • Use Date.now() so a countdown stays accurate even when ticks arrive late.
  • Save and load text with localStorage, and whole objects with JSON.stringify and JSON.parse.

A habit-timer app gets this bug report: "I clicked Start twice and my 10-minute timer finished in 5 minutes. Then I refreshed the page and my 12-day streak was gone."

That is two bugs. Every click started another timer, and both counted down the same number. And the streak lived in a JavaScript variable, which is wiped every time the page reloads. This module fixes both, and next lesson you'll build a pomodoro timer that survives a refresh.

#setTimeout runs a function later, and doesn't wait for it

Think of an oven timer. You set it for 20 minutes and go chop vegetables. You don't stand frozen in front of the oven. setTimeout works the same way: you hand the browser a function and a delay, and your code carries on immediately.

Precisely: setTimeout(callback, delay) asks the browser to call callback once, after at least delay milliseconds. It returns an id, and clearTimeout(id) cancels the call if it hasn't happened yet.

Before you look at the output, predict the order of the three lines.

Line 2 prints before line 3 even though it comes later in the file. setTimeout only schedules the callback, so the script keeps going and finishes first. The second timer is cancelled before its 200 ms are up, so its message never appears. Even a delay of 0 wouldn't change the order; Module 6 explains why.

#setInterval repeats until you tell it to stop

setInterval(callback, delay) calls the function again and again, every delay milliseconds, forever. The only way to stop it is clearInterval(id), using the id it gave you. Lose the id and you lose the off switch.

The callback can stop its own interval because tickerId was saved in a variable it can see. Every countdown you write will have this "count, then stop yourself" shape.

#The double-start bug, and the two-line fix

Every call to setInterval creates a brand-new, independent timer. If a Start button calls it on every click, two clicks means two timers both adding to the same counter. Worse, the variable that held the first id now holds the second one, so Stop can only cancel one of them.

Click Start on the buggy timer three times, then click Stop. Then do the same on the fixed one.

The buggy timer speeds up with each click, and Stop only slows it down by one interval. The fix is two lines. if (fixId !== null) return; means "a timer is already running, so do nothing", and fixId = null; after clearInterval means "there's no timer now, so Start is allowed again". Forget the second line and Start stops working after the first Stop.

#Ticks arrive late, so trust the clock

Time an egg by counting "one Mississippi, two Mississippi" while answering the phone and you'll lose count; a clock won't. Timers have the same problem: a delay is a minimum, not a promise. If the page is busy, the next tick waits. In a background tab, browsers slow timers down on purpose to save battery; Firefox waits at least a second between runs, and Chrome can drop to about once a minute for a tab that has been hidden for more than five minutes.

This program pretends the page is busy for 250 ms during the second tick. Compare the counted time with the real time.

After the busy moment, "counted" falls behind and never catches up. A countdown that subtracts 1 second per tick would show the wrong time. The fix is to remember when the countdown ends, using Date.now() (milliseconds since 1 January 1970), and work out the time left on every tick. The interval then only decides how often to redraw.

Redrawing four times a second costs almost nothing and means the display never skips a number. Math.ceil rounds 9.4 seconds up to 10, so the display reaches 0 exactly when time runs out.

🧪 Try it yourself

Start the countdown, switch to another tab for 5 seconds, then come back. The number jumps to the right value at once, because each tick asks the clock instead of counting.

#localStorage keeps strings after a refresh

Everything in your JavaScript variables disappears when the page reloads. localStorage is a small notebook the browser keeps for each website. It survives refreshes and restarts, each site gets its own (about 5 MiB), and it has one strict rule: it only stores strings.

To see it, open DevTools on a Live Server page, go to Application › Storage › Local storage, and click your site's address (in Firefox, use the Storage tab). You can read, edit, and delete keys there.

Node doesn't have localStorage, so this program builds a stand-in that follows the same rule: whatever you save is turned into a string with String(). Predict both lines before you look.

The number 12 came back as the text "12", so + 1 glued on a character and gave 121. The object became the useless text [object Object], and its data is gone. The real localStorage behaves exactly like this.

#JSON turns objects into text and back

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format that looks almost exactly like a JavaScript object. JSON.stringify(value) turns an object or array into a JSON string, and JSON.parse(text) turns it back.

The round trip keeps numbers as numbers and arrays as arrays. The last part shows what happens when the saved text isn't valid JSON: JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError. Real apps hit this when an old version saved something broken or someone edited the value in DevTools. So a good load function expects three cases: nothing saved yet, good data, and damaged data.

{ ...DEFAULTS, ...saved } copies the defaults, then lets the saved values overwrite them. If you add a new setting next month, people with older saved data still get a sensible value for it.

⚠️ Watch out

Three classic mistakes.

  1. Saving an object directly. localStorage.setItem("todos", todos) stores "[object Object]" (or, for an array, its items joined by commas). Later, JSON.parse throws SyntaxError: "[object Object]" is not valid JSON. Always wrap the value in JSON.stringify.
  2. Forgetting the first visit. getItem returns null when nothing is saved, and JSON.parse(null) returns null, so load().streak crashes with TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'streak'). Check for null and return defaults.
  3. Not clearing the id. After clearInterval(timerId), set timerId = null, or your "already running?" check will block Start forever.

📝 Note

Some lesson previews on this site run in a locked-down frame where localStorage is switched off, and touching it throws a SecurityError. Your own pages on Live Server don't have that limit. Also, never keep passwords or private data in localStorage: any script running on your page can read it.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1What does this print? console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0); console.log("C");

  • A delay of 0 doesn't run the callback right away. It still waits until the current script has finished.

  • setTimeout only schedules B. The script finishes first (A, then C), and then the callback runs.

  • Nothing can jump ahead of code that is already running, and B was scheduled after A printed.

Show answer

B. setTimeout only schedules B. The script finishes first (A, then C), and then the callback runs.

2You run localStorage.setItem("count", 9) and later localStorage.getItem("count") + 1. What do you get?

  • That would need a number, but localStorage handed back the string "9".

  • The value was stored as text. A string plus a number joins them, so you get "91". Use Number(...) to convert first.

  • NaN comes from failed maths, like Number("abc"). Here JavaScript joined the strings instead.

Show answer

B. The value was stored as text. A string plus a number joins them, so you get "91". Use Number(...) to convert first.

3In the buggy timer you click Start three times, then Stop once. What happens?

  • Stop only cancels the id stored last. The other two intervals have no variable pointing at them any more.

  • Three intervals were running; Stop cancelled one, so two are still adding to the same counter.

  • Nothing in the code subtracts. The leftover intervals keep adding.

Show answer

B. Three intervals were running; Stop cancelled one, so two are still adding to the same counter.

4Why does the countdown store endAt instead of subtracting one second on every tick?

  • A busy page or a background tab delays ticks. Working out endAt - Date.now() gives the true time left no matter how many ticks were missed.

  • It can, it just doesn't guarantee exact timing. That's the problem endAt solves.

  • Both are instant. The issue is accuracy, not speed.

Show answer

A. A busy page or a background tab delays ticks. Working out endAt - Date.now() gives the true time left no matter how many ticks were missed.

Key takeaways

  • setTimeout and setInterval schedule work and return immediately; your code keeps running.
  • Keep the id from setInterval, guard Start with if (timerId !== null) return;, and set the id back to null after clearInterval.
  • For countdowns, save the end time and compute endAt - Date.now() each tick; never count ticks.
  • localStorage stores strings only. Use JSON.stringify to save objects and JSON.parse to load them.
  • A safe load() handles three cases: nothing saved (null), good data, and damaged data (try/catch).

#Further reading

  • MDN: setInterval() (opens in a new tab): the full reference, including why the delay is only a minimum.
  • MDN: Using the Web Storage API (opens in a new tab): a short guide to localStorage with a working example page.
  • MDN: JSON.stringify() (opens in a new tab): what survives the trip to text (and what doesn't, like functions and dates).

m5-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Turn a number of milliseconds into a mm:ss display.
  • Run exactly one countdown at a time, timed with Date.now() so it stays accurate.
  • Switch between focus and break sessions when the clock reaches zero.
  • Save the timer to localStorage and restore it, mid-countdown, after a refresh.

The pomodoro technique is simple: work on one thing for 25 minutes, take a 5-minute break, repeat. The timer you'll build does that, and it fixes both bugs from the last lesson. Clicking Start ten times still runs one countdown, and refreshing the page (or closing the tab and coming back) doesn't lose your place.

Here is the finished app. In this preview a "minute" lasts one second, so a whole focus-and-break cycle takes 30 seconds. Press Start, try Pause and Reset, and let it run to zero.

This preview runs in a locked-down frame where saving is switched off, so it forgets everything when you leave the page. The copy you build in VS Code will remember.

#The plan: one state object and a handful of functions

Everything the timer needs to know lives in one object called state. The buttons never touch the page directly. They call a function that changes state, saves it, and calls render() to redraw the page from it.

There are two ways to know the time left, and the running flag picks between them. While the clock runs, the truth is endAt - Date.now(). While paused, there is no end time yet, so remainingMs holds the frozen value.

#Step 1: Make the files

Make a folder called pomodoro and open it in VS Code. Add three files.

For style.css, copy the rules from the style block at the bottom of the preview above. Leave script.js empty for now. Right-click index.html and choose Open with Live Server. You should see a pink card showing 25:00 with two buttons that do nothing yet.

Two accessibility choices are already in the HTML. role="timer" tells screen readers this number is a clock, and timers are not read aloud on every change (hearing "24:59, 24:58…" would be unbearable). The status line has aria-live="polite", so when it changes to "Time for a break", a screen reader announces it once.

#Step 2: Show milliseconds as mm:ss

Everything in the timer is measured in milliseconds, because that's what Date.now() returns. People want to read 24:59. This function does the conversion, and it is pure (no page, no clock), so you can test it on its own.

padStart(2, "0") adds a leading zero to one-digit numbers, so 1 minute shows as 01. Math.ceil rounds partial seconds up: with 400 ms left the display still says 00:01, and it only shows 00:00 when time has truly run out. With Math.floor the clock would sit on 00:00 for most of a second before anything happened.

#Step 3: Start and pause, with exactly one interval

Put this at the top of script.js, followed by the formatTime function from Step 2.

Next come the state and the functions that run the clock. start() turns "time left" into a fixed end time; pause() does the reverse.

Save, and Live Server reloads the page. Now Start counts down, the button turns into Pause, and pausing freezes the time. Start again and it continues from the frozen value. Click Start-Pause-Start as fast as you can: the countdown never speeds up.

That's thanks to two separate guards. if (state.running) return; in start() protects the logic (don't recompute the end time while running). if (timerId !== null) return; in startTicking() protects the mechanics (never create a second interval). Each one is a single line, and together they make the double-start bug impossible.

render() also writes the time into document.title, so the countdown shows in the browser tab while you work in another one.

#Step 4: Switch between focus and break

When time runs out, the app should count the session (if it was a focus one), flip the mode, and wait for the next Start. Replace tick() and add finishSession() and reset().

Nobody wants to wait 25 minutes to test this. Set SECONDS_PER_MINUTE = 1 while you work, so a focus session lasts 25 seconds. Let it reach zero and you should see:

The card turns green because render() sets data-mode="break" on it, and the CSS rule .app[data-mode="break"] picks a different background.

#Step 5: Save after every change, load once at the start

Add these two functions near the top of the file, under durationFor, and replace the let state = { … } object with let state = load();.

Then call save() just before render() in start, pause, reset, and finishSession. Every change is now written down the moment it happens.

Here is load() tested in Node with a stand-in for localStorage, covering the three cases from the last lesson: nothing saved, good data, and damaged data.

On the first visit getItem returns null, JSON.parse(null) gives null, and spreading null adds nothing, so you get a fresh state. The saved data only had two fields, and the defaults filled in the rest. The damaged text threw a SyntaxError, which catch turned into a fresh start instead of a blank page.

Finally, a refresh may happen while the clock is running. endAt is a moment on the clock, so it means the same thing after a reload. Put this at the very bottom of the file, replacing the lone render();:

Now test it properly. Start a session and refresh: the countdown carries on. Open DevTools, go to Application › Storage › Local storage, and click your Live Server address to see the pomodoro key with its JSON. Double-click the value, change it to {oops, and refresh. The app starts fresh instead of crashing. One more nice side effect: Live Server reloads the page every time you save a file, and the timer no longer loses its place when that happens.

💡 Tip

If you switch SECONDS_PER_MINUTE from 1 back to 60, click Reset once. The saved remainingMs was measured with the old setting.

#The finished script.js

Check your understanding

3 questions

1A focus session is running. You close the tab, come back 10 minutes later, and the timer shows the right time. Why?

  • Closing or refreshing a page stops all of its timers. Nothing ran while you were away.

  • On load, timeLeft() works out endAt - Date.now(). Ten minutes later, that subtraction gives exactly 10 minutes less.

  • localStorage only stores text. It never changes a value on its own.

Show answer

B. On load, timeLeft() works out endAt - Date.now(). Ten minutes later, that subtraction gives exactly 10 minutes less.

2Why does the interval run every 250 ms instead of every 1,000 ms?

  • Ticks can be late. With one tick a second, a late one could make the display skip a number or lag behind. Four cheap redraws a second hide that.

  • The timer doesn't count ticks at all. The time left always comes from endAt - Date.now().

  • Any delay works. 250 is a choice for smoothness.

Show answer

A. Ticks can be late. With one tick a second, a late one could make the display skip a number or lag behind. Four cheap redraws a second hide that.

3Why does load() return { ...freshState(), ...saved } instead of just saved?

  • JSON.parse already did that. The spread is about which fields end up in the result.

  • If an older version of your app saved only mode and sessions, the fresh state supplies running, endAt, and the rest, and nothing is ever undefined.

  • It's slightly more work, not less. It's there for safety.

Show answer

B. If an older version of your app saved only mode and sessions, the fresh state supplies running, endAt, and the rest, and nothing is ever undefined.

Key takeaways

  • One state object holds everything the timer knows, and every button follows the same pattern: change state, save(), render().
  • Store a running countdown as an end time (endAt). It stays correct across late ticks, background tabs, and page reloads.
  • Two small guards (state.running and timerId !== null) make double starts impossible.
  • load() merges saved data over fresh defaults inside try/catch, so first visits and damaged data both start cleanly.
  • Speed up time while testing (SECONDS_PER_MINUTE = 1) instead of waiting 25 minutes.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Long breaks. After every fourth focus session, make the break 15 minutes. state.sessions % 4 === 0 tells you when.
  • Custom lengths. Add a small form for focus and break minutes, validate that each is a whole number from 1 to 90, and save the choice with the rest of the state.
  • A sound at zero. Browsers only allow audio after the person has interacted with the page, and pressing Start counts, so new Audio("ding.mp3").play() in finishSession() will work.
  • A keyboard shortcut. Let the Space bar toggle the timer from anywhere on the page, but skip it when a button already has focus, or one press will toggle twice.
  • Daily history. Save sessions per date ({ "2026-11-15": 4 }) and show a small table of the last seven days.

#Further reading

  • Chrome DevTools: view and edit local storage (opens in a new tab): every way to inspect, edit, and clear what your app saved.
  • MDN: String.prototype.padStart() (opens in a new tab): the leading-zero trick, with more examples.
  • MDN: ARIA timer role (opens in a new tab): why a countdown shouldn't be announced on every change, and when it should.

m5-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write countdowns that stop themselves with clearInterval.
  • Restart a setTimeout correctly with clearTimeout.
  • Save and restore settings, lists, and drafts with localStorage and JSON, including the first-visit and damaged-data cases.
  • Find and fix the classic timer bugs: double starts, drift, and timers that never stop.

Make a new folder for each browser exercise with an index.html (and a script.js if you like), and open it with Live Server. The Node exercises run as they are; you can also paste them into the DevTools Console. Try each one properly before you open the solution.

#Warm-up: predict, then check

Check your understanding

2 questions

1What order do the letters print in? setTimeout(() => console.log("A"), 200); setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 100); console.log("C");

  • That's the order in the file, but neither timer callback can run before the script finishes.

  • C is right to go first, but the 100 ms timer fires before the 200 ms one.

  • C runs immediately. Then the shorter timer (B, 100 ms) fires, then A at 200 ms.

Show answer

C. C runs immediately. Then the shorter timer (B, 100 ms) fires, then A at 200 ms.

2After localStorage.setItem("darkMode", false), does if (localStorage.getItem("darkMode")) { … } run its body?

  • The value was stored as the string "false". Any non-empty string is truthy, so the if runs. Compare with the string instead: === "true".

  • It would be skipped for the real false, but localStorage handed back the text "false".

Show answer

A. The value was stored as the string "false". Any non-empty string is truthy, so the if runs. Compare with the string instead: === "true".

#Exercise 1: Liftoff

Write a Node program that prints 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 (one every 200 ms) and then Liftoff!, and then stops. Use setInterval and clearInterval, not five setTimeout calls.

Need a hint?

Keep a count variable outside the interval. Each tick, either print and subtract, or print Liftoff! and clear the interval. Save the id that setInterval returns, or you can't stop it.

Show solution

The interval checks count before printing, so the sixth tick prints Liftoff! and stops the interval. Without clearInterval(id), it would print Liftoff! forever.

#Exercise 2: A message that hides itself

Make a Save button. Clicking it shows the text "Saved!" for 2 seconds, then hides it. If someone clicks again while the message is showing, the 2 seconds start over, so the message never disappears early.

Need a hint?

Click once, wait 1.5 seconds, click again. A plain setTimeout per click lets the first timer hide the message only half a second after the second click. Keep the timeout id in a variable and call clearTimeout on it before setting a new one.

Show solution

clearTimeout(null) does nothing, so the first click is safe. Every later click cancels the pending hide and schedules a fresh one, so the message stays up for 2 seconds after the last click.

#Exercise 3: Remember dark mode

The theme switch from Module 4 forgets your choice every time the page reloads. Build a "Dark mode" checkbox that switches the page to a dark theme and is still ticked after a refresh.

Need a hint?

Store the string "dark" or "light", not a boolean (remember the warm-up). On load, read the value, set checkbox.checked, and apply the class. Put your storage calls in try/catch so the page still works when storage is blocked.

Show solution

?? "light" handles the first visit, when getItem returns null. classList.toggle("dark", condition) adds the class when the condition is true and removes it when false, so one line covers both themes. In this preview the choice resets when you leave; on Live Server it survives a refresh.

#Exercise 4: Save a whole list

Write two functions. saveList(key, items) stores an array. loadList(key) returns the array, or an empty array [] if nothing is saved, the text is damaged, or the saved value isn't an array. Test them with the stand-in storage below (Node has no localStorage).

Need a hint?

JSON.parse goes inside try. After parsing, Array.isArray(value) tells you whether you really got a list. JSON.parse('{"a":1}') parses fine but gives an object, which would crash any code that calls .map on it.

Show solution

On the first visit JSON.parse(null) returns null, which isn't an array, so you get []. In the browser, replace storage with localStorage and the functions work unchanged.

#Exercise 5: Fix the stopwatch

This stopwatch has three bugs. Click Start twice, try Reset while it runs, and leave it in a background tab for a minute. Find all three, then rewrite it so it can't double-start, Reset really stops it, and the time is measured with Date.now() instead of counted ticks.

Need a hint?

The three bugs: Start has no guard; Reset never calls clearInterval; and tenths + 1 assumes every tick is exactly on time. For the third, keep two numbers: elapsedBefore (time from earlier runs) and startedAt (when the current run began). The time shown is elapsedBefore + (Date.now() - startedAt).

Show solution

Bug 3 is fixed by elapsed(): the interval only redraws, and the clock supplies the time. Stop "banks" the time into elapsedBefore before setting id = null, because elapsed() uses id to decide whether the stopwatch is running.

#Exercise 6: Autosave a draft

Make a textarea that saves its text to localStorage 1 second after the person stops typing, not on every key press. Show "Saving…" while waiting and "Saved" once it's stored, and restore the draft when the page loads.

Need a hint?

On every input event, cancel the previous timeout and start a new 1-second one. Only the last timeout survives, so it fires once, after a second with no typing. This pattern is called debouncing. The diagram below shows the timeline.

Show solution

The draft is plain text, so it needs no JSON. To convince yourself that only one save happens, here is the same debounce in Node, with key presses simulated 100 ms apart:

Three key presses, one save, with the final text. Without clearTimeout you'd see three saves.

#Challenge: a practice streak

Build a page with an I practiced today button and a line that says "Current streak: 4 days". Save the dates as an array of strings like "2026-11-15". Pressing the button twice on one day must not count twice. The streak counts consecutive days ending today, or ending yesterday if you haven't practised yet today (so the streak doesn't drop to 0 at midnight). It must survive a refresh.

Need a hint?

Write two pure functions you can test in Node first: dateKey(date) turns a Date into "YYYY-MM-DD" (use getFullYear, getMonth() + 1, getDate, and padStart), and currentStreak(days, today) walks backwards one day at a time while the day is in the list. date.setDate(date.getDate() - 1) steps back a day and handles month boundaries for you. Put the days in a Set to check them quickly and to ignore repeats.

Show solution

The logic, tested with fixed dates that cross from October into November:

In the page, load the array with your loadList from Exercise 4. The button adds dateKey(new Date()) only if it isn't already in the list, saves, and re-renders currentStreak(days, new Date()). Months in new Date(2026, 10, 2) count from 0, so 10 is November, a classic source of off-by-one bugs.

What you'll learn

  • Explain why JavaScript never freezes while it waits, using the call stack and the event loop.
  • Predict the order of synchronous code, promise callbacks, and timer callbacks.
  • Write async functions that await promises and catch their errors with try/catch.
  • Load JSON with fetch, check response.ok, and show loading, success, and error states.

Open the DevTools Console on any page you've made with Live Server and type this:

You'd expect GitHub's mascot's profile. What you get is this:

The data lives on a server, perhaps thousands of kilometres away, and it takes a moment to arrive. JavaScript refuses to stand still while it waits, so fetch hands you a promise, a placeholder for a value that isn't ready yet. Here is how that waiting works, and how to get at the data when it lands.

#JavaScript does one thing at a time, so it never waits around

Picture a restaurant with one cook. A good cook doesn't stare at the oven for 12 minutes. They put the pizza in, set a timer, and start the next order. When the timer rings, they take the pizza out as soon as their hands are free.

JavaScript in a page is that cook. It has one call stack: one piece of code running at a time, always to the end. The waiting (timers, network requests, listening for clicks) is done by the browser, outside your code. When a wait is over, the browser puts the callback in a queue. The event loop hands the next queued callback to JavaScript whenever the stack is empty.

There are two queues. Promise callbacks go in the microtask queue, which is emptied completely before the next ordinary task (like a timer callback) gets a turn. Predict the order of these four lines before you look.

The two plain console.log lines run first, because the current script always finishes. Then the microtask (the promise callback) runs, and only then the timer callback, even though its delay was 0. The flip side: if your own code runs a long loop, nothing else can happen. No clicks are handled and the page doesn't redraw until the stack is empty. That's the "busy page" from Module 5 that made timer ticks late.

#A promise is an order number for a value that isn't ready yet

At a sandwich shop you get an order number. Right now it's pending. Later it either becomes a sandwich (fulfilled) or the cashier tells you they're out of bread (rejected). Either way it only happens once: a fulfilled order never turns into a rejection afterwards.

You'll rarely create promises yourself, because fetch and other browser features give you one. Building one by hand shows the shape, though. This fake weather service answers after 200 ms.

.then runs when the promise is fulfilled and receives the value; .catch runs when it's rejected and receives the error. Both requests were waiting at the same time, which is why "Asked for two forecasts..." printed first.

#async and await let you write it top to bottom

Chains of .then get hard to read. Inside a function marked async, you can write await promise instead. It pauses that function until the promise settles, then gives you the value, or throws the error so try/catch can handle it.

"Meanwhile" printed before the toast popped. await paused makeToast, not the whole program, so the rest of the script kept running. One more rule: an async function always returns a promise, even when you return "toast". That's why breakfast had to await makeToast() to get the actual string.

#fetch in two steps: the response, then the body

fetch(url) returns a promise for a response. The response arrives as soon as the server sends its status and headers, which may be before the whole body has downloaded. Reading the body is a second wait: response.json() returns another promise that gives you the parsed data.

Put that in a script.js served by Live Server and the Console shows (the numbers may change over time):

This page can't run fetch for you (its examples have no network access), but your own pages can. Open the Network panel in DevTools while it runs and you'll see the request to api.github.com and its JSON reply.

#A 404 is not an error to fetch

Here is the trap that catches nearly everyone. If you ask GitHub for a user that doesn't exist, it replies with status 404 and a small JSON body saying "Not Found". To fetch, that's a perfectly good response, so the promise is fulfilled, not rejected. This program uses a stand-in for fetch that answers exactly like GitHub does for a missing user.

No error, just undefined on the screen. The fix is to check response.ok, which is true only for statuses 200 to 299, and throw your own error otherwise:

fetch itself only rejects when there's no response at all: you're offline, the address doesn't exist, or the browser blocked the request. In Chrome that error is TypeError: Failed to fetch. So there are two kinds of failure, and one try/catch around await getUser(...) handles both.

#Show every state: loading, success, and error

A request takes time and might fail, so the page has to show something in each case. Leave out the loading state and people click again and again; leave out the error state and they stare at a blank box. This preview fakes a slow server (1.5 seconds) so you can see all three. Tick the box to make it fail.

⚠️ Watch out

The three async bugs you'll write at least once.

  1. Forgetting await. const response = fetch(url); stores the promise, not the response, so response.json() fails with TypeError: response.json is not a function.
  2. Using await outside an async function. In a normal script this is SyntaxError: await is only valid in async functions and the top level bodies of modules. Add async to the function that contains the await.
  3. Trusting every response. Without if (!response.ok), a 404 or 500 sails through and your page shows undefined.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1What does this print? console.log(1); setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3)); console.log(4);

  • That's the order in the file, but both callbacks must wait for the script to finish.

  • The script part is right, but promise callbacks (microtasks) run before timer callbacks.

  • The script finishes (1, 4), the microtask queue empties (3), and then the timer task runs (2).

Show answer

C. The script finishes (1, 4), the microtask queue empties (3), and then the timer task runs (2).

2You fetch a GitHub user that doesn't exist. What happens to the promise?

  • The server answered, so fetch succeeded. It's your job to check response.ok.

  • fetch only rejects when no response arrives at all, for example when you're offline.

  • You always get a response object. Its body holds GitHub's "Not Found" message.

Show answer

A. The server answered, so fetch succeeded. It's your job to check response.ok.

3What happens when you run const user = fetch(url).json();?

  • fetch(url) is a promise, and promises don't have a .json() method.

  • You need the response first: const response = await fetch(url);, then await response.json().

  • That would be true of response.json(), but here .json() is called on the promise from fetch, which fails.

Show answer

B. You need the response first: const response = await fetch(url);, then await response.json().

4In the fact loader, why does button.disabled = false go in finally?

  • finally runs last, after try or catch has finished.

  • If it were only at the end of try, one failed request would leave the button disabled forever.

  • You can change any property anywhere. The point is to write it once for both outcomes.

Show answer

B. If it were only at the end of try, one failed request would leave the button disabled forever.

Key takeaways

  • JavaScript runs one thing at a time; the browser does the waiting and queues callbacks. Promise callbacks run before timer callbacks.
  • A promise is pending, then fulfilled or rejected, exactly once. await pauses only the async function it's in.
  • fetch takes two waits: await fetch(url) for the response, then await response.json() for the data.
  • fetch rejects only when there's no response. Check response.ok and throw for 404s and 500s.
  • Every request needs a loading state, a success state, and an error state with a way to try again.

#Further reading

  • MDN: Using promises (opens in a new tab): chaining, error handling, and how async/await relates to .then.
  • MDN: Using the Fetch API (opens in a new tab): every part of a request and a response, including headers and status checks.
  • javascript.info: Event loop (opens in a new tab): a careful written explanation of tasks and microtasks, with exercises.

m6-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Read an API's JSON before writing code against it.
  • Write a getJSON helper that turns bad HTTP statuses into errors.
  • Show a loading state, then the profile, or a message that tells the person what to do next.
  • Build page content from API data with textContent, so text from strangers can't inject HTML.
  • Run two requests at the same time with Promise.all.

GitHub has a free public API. Ask it about any username and it answers with JSON, with no account or key needed. You'll build a page where someone types a username and gets back the person's avatar, name, bio, stats, and five recent repositories. Then you'll make it behave well when things go wrong, which is most of the work in any app that talks to a server.

Here's the finished viewer. This page can't reach the internet from its previews, so this copy answers from sample data saved from the real API: try octocat, any other name (not found), and offline (no connection). The version you build on Live Server talks to GitHub for real.

#Step 1: Look at the data before you write code

Open https://api.github.com/users/octocat (opens in a new tab) in a new browser tab. You'll see the raw JSON that your code will receive. It has about 30 fields; these are the ones the viewer uses:

Notice "bio": null. Plenty of users have no bio, and some have no name either, so the code must handle null. Now change the address to a username that can't exist, like https://api.github.com/users/no-such-user-zz-404. GitHub sends status 404 and this body:

Five minutes reading real responses saves an hour of guessing why something is undefined.

#Step 2: Make the page

Make a github-viewer folder with an index.html, a style.css, and an empty script.js.

Copy the CSS from the style block at the end of the preview. The status paragraph will carry every message ("Looking up…", "not found", "offline"), and aria-live="polite" makes screen readers announce each one. The profile article starts hidden because there's nothing to show yet.

#Step 3: A getJSON helper that refuses bad answers

Last lesson showed that fetch happily fulfills its promise for a 404. You'll make several requests, so write the check once, in a helper. It throws an error that carries the status, so later code can decide what to tell the person.

You can test this without a network by swapping in a fake fetch for a moment. This Node program tries three fake answers: a success, a 404, and no connection at all.

The 404 now becomes a real error with status: 404. The offline case is a TypeError with no status at all, and that difference is exactly what Step 5 will use.

#Step 4: Show "Looking up…", then the profile

When the form is submitted, the handler stops the page from reloading, checks the input, switches on the loading state, and waits. Add these to script.js:

make is a tiny helper so each element takes one line. replaceChildren swaps out everything inside the article in one go, so searching twice never stacks two profiles. user.name ?? user.login falls back to the username when name is null, and the same trick gives an empty bio a friendly default.

Every piece of text goes in through textContent, never innerHTML. Bios and repository names are typed by strangers. If someone's bio were <img src=x onerror="alert('hacked')">, innerHTML would turn it into a real element and run the code; textContent shows it as harmless characters.

#Step 5: Turn errors into messages people can act on

"Request failed with status 404" means nothing to most people. Each kind of failure deserves its own sentence that says what to do next. GitHub allows 60 requests an hour from one address without signing in, and after that it answers 403 or 429.

The order of the checks matters. Specific statuses come first, then "any other status", and last the case with no status at all, which can only mean the request never got an answer.

Now the submit handler ties it together:

#Step 6: Ask for the profile and the repositories at once

The repositories come from a second address, /users/octocat/repos. The two requests don't depend on each other, so there's no reason to wait for one before starting the other. Promise.all takes an array of promises and waits for all of them, giving back their results in the same order.

If each request takes 300 ms, awaiting them one after the other takes about 600 ms; together they take about 300. If either one fails, Promise.all rejects straight away with that error, so the catch in the submit handler still works. encodeURIComponent makes sure odd input like spaces or ? can't break the address. The query string ?sort=updated&per_page=5 asks GitHub for the five most recently updated repositories.

#Step 7: Break it on purpose with DevTools

Open the viewer with Live Server and look up octocat. Then open DevTools and go to the Network panel.

  1. Click Fetch/XHR to hide everything except your two API requests. Click one to see its status, headers, and the JSON under Response.
  2. In the throttling drop-down (it says No throttling), pick Slow 4G and search again. Now you can actually read "Looking up octocat…" and see the button stay disabled.
  3. Pick Offline and search again. You should get "Couldn't reach GitHub. Check your internet connection and try again."
  4. Set it back to No throttling, then search for a name that can't exist.

#The finished script.js

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does renderProfile put the bio in with textContent instead of innerHTML?

  • innerHTML can set text too. The difference is what happens to text that looks like HTML.

  • textContent always shows characters as characters, so a bio containing <img onerror=…> is displayed, not run.

  • It works with any string. That's exactly why it's risky with untrusted text.

Show answer

B. textContent always shows characters as characters, so a bio containing <img onerror=…> is displayed, not run.

2What does Promise.all buy you in loadProfile?

  • Awaiting them one after another would add the two waits together.

  • Promise.all never retries. If either request fails, the whole thing rejects with that error.

  • Each request still counts. Two requests per search means 30 searches an hour, not 60.

Show answer

A. Awaiting them one after another would add the two waits together.

3Someone loses their Wi-Fi and searches. Which message do they see, and why?

  • No response means no 404 either. fetch rejected before any status existed.

  • fetch rejects with a TypeError that has no status property, so every status check is skipped and the last line runs.

  • error.status is undefined, not 0, so if (error.status) is false.

Show answer

B. fetch rejects with a TypeError that has no status property, so every status check is skipped and the last line runs.

Key takeaways

  • Read the real JSON first. It tells you the field names and which ones can be null.
  • Put the response.ok check in one getJSON helper and attach the status to the error you throw.
  • Disable the button and show a loading message while waiting; use finally to switch it back on.
  • Give each failure (not found, rate limited, server trouble, offline) its own message that says what to do.
  • Use textContent for anything that came from an API, and Promise.all for requests that don't depend on each other.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Recent searches. Save the last five usernames to localStorage and show them as buttons that search again when clicked.
  • Member since. new Date(user.created_at).getFullYear() gives the year the account was made.
  • Requests left. GitHub reports your remaining quota in a response header. Read it with response.headers.get("x-ratelimit-remaining") and show it in small print.
  • Compare two users. Two inputs, two sets of requests, all four in one Promise.all, shown side by side.
  • Link the repositories. Each repo object has an html_url. Make each list item a link that opens the repository.

#Further reading

  • GitHub Docs: REST API endpoints for users (opens in a new tab): every field in the user object, with example responses.
  • GitHub Docs: Rate limits for the REST API (opens in a new tab): the 60-an-hour limit, the headers that report it, and what to do when you hit it.
  • MDN: Promise.all() (opens in a new tab): how it orders results and what happens when one promise rejects.

m6-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write promise-based helpers like wait(ms) and use them with await in loops.
  • Convert .then chains to async/await with try/catch.
  • Retry failed work, time sequential and parallel requests, and add a timeout.
  • Fetch a real API with a loading state, and make sure only the latest request updates the page.

Most of these run in Node with fake, delayed "servers", so you can test async logic without a network or rate limits. Exercise 5 and the challenge use a real API in the browser, served by Live Server.

#Warm-up: predict, then check

Check your understanding

2 questions

1What does this print? async function f() { console.log("B"); await null; console.log("D"); } console.log("A"); f(); console.log("C");

  • An async function starts running straight away. It only steps aside when it reaches await.

  • f() prints B immediately, pauses at await, the script prints C, and then f resumes and prints D.

  • await always pauses, even for a value that's already there, so C gets in first.

Show answer

B. f() prints B immediately, pauses at await, the script prints C, and then f resumes and prints D.

2What does console.log(getAge()) show if async function getAge() { return 15; }?

  • An async function wraps whatever it returns in a promise.

  • Chrome shows it as Promise {<fulfilled>: 15}. Use await getAge() (inside an async function) or .then to get the number.

  • The function does return something: a promise holding 15.

Show answer

B. Chrome shows it as Promise {<fulfilled>: 15}. Use await getAge() (inside an async function) or .then to get the number.

#Exercise 1: Countdown with await

Write a wait(ms) function that returns a promise fulfilled after ms milliseconds. Then use it inside a for loop to print 3, 2, 1, and Go!, 300 ms apart. No setInterval allowed.

Need a hint?

new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms)) is the whole of wait. The loop has to be inside an async function so it can await wait(300) on each pass.

Show solution

Compare this with the setInterval liftoff from Module 5: no ids, no clearInterval, and the loop reads like the countdown sounds. await inside a loop is the natural way to do one slow thing after another.

#Exercise 2: Untangle the .then chain

This works, but the nesting makes it hard to follow. Rewrite showStudent with async/await and try/catch so it prints exactly the same thing.

Need a hint?

Each .then((x) => …) becomes const x = await …;. The .catch becomes a catch (error) block around the whole body.

Show solution

Both student and cls are ordinary variables in one scope now, which is why the nesting disappears. The second getClass has to wait for the first result anyway (it needs student.classId), so awaiting them one after the other is right here.

#Exercise 3: Try again before giving up

Servers sometimes fail for a moment. Write withRetry(task, attempts), which calls the async function task and returns its result. If it throws, wait 200 ms and try again, up to attempts tries in total. If every try fails, throw the last error. Test it with this flaky fake, which fails twice and then works:

Need a hint?

Use a for loop with a try/catch inside. Write return await task();, not return task();. Without await, the rejected promise escapes the try before it has a chance to fail, and the catch never sees it.

Show solution

Only retry errors that might go away. A 404 will be a 404 every time, and a 403 from a rate limit gets worse if you hammer the server, so real code checks error.status before retrying.

#Exercise 4: One by one, or all at once?

A dashboard needs weather, news, and scores. Each fake request takes 300 ms. Write oneByOne(), which awaits the three in turn, and allAtOnce(), which uses Promise.all. Time both with Date.now(), rounded to the nearest 100 ms.

Need a hint?

Start the clock with const start = Date.now() before the work and subtract afterwards. Math.round(ms / 100) * 100 rounds to the nearest 100. A small time(label, fn) helper keeps the measuring code in one place.

Show solution

Promise.all gets all three requests going before waiting for any of them, and its results come back in the order you listed them, not the order they finished. Use it whenever requests don't need each other's answers.

#Exercise 5: A random dog, for real

Use the free Dog CEO API (opens in a new tab) to make a Show me a dog button. Each click fetches https://dog.ceo/api/breeds/image/random and shows the photo. The answer looks like this:

Requirements: disable the button and show "Fetching a dog…" while waiting; give the image useful alt text that names the breed (it's in the URL); and show a friendly message if anything fails, including an answer whose status isn't "success".

Need a hint?

The breed is the fifth piece when you split the URL on / (index 4): "hound-english". Test that function in Node before you touch the page. Check response.ok first, then data.status, and throw an error in either case so one catch handles everything.

Show solution

The breed helper, tested on real URLs from the API:

The page:

This API reports problems in two ways at once: an HTTP status and a status field in the JSON. Checking both costs one line. For a smoother look, clear the loading message in the image's load event instead, since the photo itself can take a moment to download after the JSON arrives.

#Exercise 6: Only the latest search wins

A search box sends a request on every key press. The person types o, then oc, then octo. The requests take different amounts of time, and the slow oc request arrives last, so the screen shows results for oc even though the box says octo. Run this to see the bug, then fix onType so that only results for the most recent request are shown.

Need a hint?

Give each request a number. Keep a variable latest outside the function and increase it at the start of every call; save a copy in a local mine. When the results come back, show them only if mine === latest.

Show solution

Each call remembers its own mine (it's a local variable), while latest is shared. By the time the slow oc results arrive, latest is 3 and mine is 2, so they're thrown away. This is exactly the "dashboard shows stale data" bug that real apps ship with, and it only shows up when the network is uneven, so test with throttling on.

#Challenge: Give up after 3 seconds

A request that hangs forever leaves your app stuck on "Loading…". Add a time limit to the GitHub viewer from the last lesson: if GitHub hasn't answered in 3 seconds, show "GitHub is taking too long. Try again."

First, build the idea in Node with Promise.race, which settles as soon as the first of its promises does. Write withTimeout(promise, ms) and test it with a fast (100 ms) and a slow (800 ms) fake, using a 500 ms limit.

Then use the browser's built-in version. AbortSignal.timeout(ms) makes a signal that cancels the request itself, and fetch then rejects with an error named "TimeoutError". To test it, use the Network panel's throttling menu, choose Custom › Add…, and create a profile with a latency of 4000 ms.

Need a hint?

For withTimeout, race the real promise against one that only ever rejects, after ms milliseconds. For the browser, pass { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3000) } as the second argument to fetch, and add an if (error.name === "TimeoutError") case to your message function.

Show solution

In the viewer, change one line of getJSON and add one check to messageFor:

Put the new check first in messageFor. Promise.race only stops waiting; the slow request carries on in the background. AbortSignal.timeout actually cancels it, which is why the browser version is better for fetch.

m7-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Keep everything that can change in one state object and redraw the page from it with render().
  • Store only the facts and calculate everything else.
  • Throw errors when a function can't do its job, and catch them where you can show a helpful message.
  • Guard against missing data with ?. and ??, and know why ?? is safer than || for defaults.
  • Split a program into modules with export and import.

A browser game shows Score: 0 after you press Restart. You score one point and it says Score: 4. Try it: click +1 point three times, then Restart, then +1 point again.

The score lives in two places: the variable score and the text on the page. Restart updated one and forgot the other, so they disagree. In a small demo you'd spot it at once. In an app with a score, a timer, a question number, and a high score, each stored in a variable and in the page, bugs like this are everywhere.

#One state object, one render() function

Think of a sports scoreboard. The official scorer keeps the real score on a sheet, and the big screen only displays what's on the sheet. Nobody climbs up and changes the screen by hand. If the screen is wrong, you fix the sheet and redraw.

You've already done part of this: the to-do list in Module 3 drew itself from an array with a render function. Here the idea becomes a rule for the whole app, in three parts:

  1. Everything that can change lives in one object, state. That's the sheet.
  2. One function, render(), updates the page to match state. That's the screen.
  3. Event handlers never touch the page. They change state, then call render().

Here's the same game following the rules. Restart replaces the whole state with a fresh one, so there's nothing left to forget.

Notice that the HTML doesn't even contain a starting score; the first render() fills it in. If you add a fifth thing to track later, you add it to createInitialState and render, and Restart handles it automatically.

#Store the facts, calculate everything else

If you store total, done, and percent next to a list of tasks, you have to remember to update all three every time a task changes. Miss one and they disagree, the same bug as before. Instead, store only the list and derive the rest whenever you need it.

Change one task and every number is right automatically, because none of them was stored. render() calls summarize(state.tasks) each time it runs.

There's a second trap hiding in "start fresh". Assigning an object to a new variable doesn't copy it; both names point at the same object. Predict what the first line prints.

Changing state.score changed START too, so "restarting" from it brought back the old score. A function like createInitialState() builds a brand-new object on every call, which is why the game above uses one.

#Throw errors on purpose, catch them where you can help

Some functions can't do their job with the input they're given. Returning a strange value (like -1 or undefined) hides the problem until something breaks far away. Throwing an error stops right there and says exactly what went wrong.

throw jumps straight out of the function, skipping the return, and lands in the nearest catch. RangeError is one of JavaScript's built-in error types; plain Error works too. The question is where to catch. Usually that's the event handler, the one place that knows how to show a message on the page. Functions deeper down just throw and let it travel up.

These are the errors you'll meet most often, and what they usually mean:

Error Usually means
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name') You used x.name, but x was undefined: missing data, or a wrong index.
ReferenceError: scroe is not defined A typo in a name, or a variable used outside the scope where it exists.
SyntaxError: "[object Object]" is not valid JSON JSON.parse got text that isn't JSON.

⚠️ Watch out

An empty catch {} makes the error vanish without a trace. Only write one when you've decided what should happen instead, like the "storage is blocked, keep going without saving" case in Module 5. Otherwise, at least show a message or console.error(error).

#Guard against data you didn't create

Data from an API, from localStorage, or from a form can be missing pieces. Optional chaining, ?., stops and gives undefined instead of crashing when something along the path is null or undefined. The nullish operator, ??, then supplies a default.

Without ?., the third object would crash with TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'name'). The last two lines show why ?? beats || for defaults: || replaces every falsy value, so a volume someone deliberately set to 0 jumps back to 50. ?? only replaces null and undefined.

A guard clause handles the bad case first and leaves early, so the rest of the function can assume good data:

#Split your code into modules

Once script.js passes a few hundred lines, finding things gets slow. Modules let each file hold one job and share only what it chooses. A file marks what it shares with export, and another file asks for it with import.

addPoint returns a new object instead of changing the old one. A function that only takes values and returns values, never touching the page, is easy to test in Node, and you'll use that heavily in the next lesson. A few rules come with modules:

  • They need a server. Double-click index.html so it opens as a file:// address and the Console says Access to script at 'file:///…/main.js' from origin 'null' has been blocked by CORS policy. Open it with Live Server instead.
  • Write the path in full. "./state.js", with the ./ and the .js. Browsers don't guess.
  • Each module has its own scope. Top-level variables are no longer global, so onclick="addPoint()" in your HTML can't find anything. Use addEventListener.
  • They wait for the page. Module scripts are deferred automatically, so you don't need defer.

If you import a name a module doesn't export (a typo, or a missing export), the Console shows SyntaxError: The requested module './state.js' does not provide an export named 'addPiont', and nothing in main.js runs.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1In the buggy score game, what's the best fix for Restart?

  • It fixes this bug, but the next value you add (lives, a timer) can be forgotten the same way.

  • Restart then can't miss anything: every field gets its starting value and the page is redrawn from it.

  • That throws away everything, including things you wanted to keep, like a high score.

Show answer

B. Restart then can't miss anything: every field gets its starting value and the page is redrawn from it.

2Someone saved volume: 0. What does const volume = saved.volume || 50; give?

  • That's what ?? would give. || treats 0 as "missing" because 0 is falsy.

  • || replaces any falsy value: 0, "", false, null, and undefined. Use ?? to keep a real 0.

  • The || operator always produces one side or the other, and here the right side is 50.

Show answer

B. || replaces any falsy value: 0, "", false, null, and undefined. Use ?? to keep a real 0.

3Your page uses <script type="module" src="main.js">. You double-click index.html and nothing works. Why?

  • Every current browser supports modules.

  • The Console shows a CORS error. Serving the folder with Live Server gives the page an http:// address, and the modules load.

  • Modules are deferred automatically; defer would change nothing.

Show answer

B. The Console shows a CORS error. Serving the folder with Live Server gives the page an http:// address, and the modules load.

4What does this print? const initial = { score: 0 }; let state = initial; state.score = 5; state = initial; console.log(state.score);

  • That would need initial to be a separate copy, but state = initial only made a second name for it.

  • state.score = 5 changed the one shared object, so initial.score is 5 as well.

  • The property exists; it just holds the changed value.

Show answer

B. state.score = 5 changed the one shared object, so initial.score is 5 as well.

Key takeaways

  • Keep every changing value in one state object; events change state, and render() redraws the page from it.
  • Store facts, not totals. Derive counts and percentages inside render().
  • Start over with a function that builds a new object; assigning an object never copies it.
  • Throw an error when a function can't do its job, and catch it where you can tell the person what happened.
  • Use ?. for paths that might be missing and ?? for defaults that keep real zeros and empty strings.
  • Modules (export, import, type="module") need a server, full ./file.js paths, and addEventListener instead of onclick attributes.

#Further reading

  • MDN: JavaScript modules (opens in a new tab): a complete guide with working examples, including the file:// problem.
  • MDN: try...catch (opens in a new tab): how catch and finally behave, including when finally overrides a return.
  • MDN: Optional chaining (?.) (opens in a new tab): every place ?. works, including method calls and array indexes.
