m7-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Store quiz questions as data and check them before the game starts.
  • Describe the whole game with one state object and four small update functions.
  • Test the game logic in Node before any page exists.
  • Draw every screen from state with render(), using one click listener for all buttons.
  • Keep keyboard focus in a sensible place, save the best score, and split the code into modules.

The quiz below reviews this course so far. Play it once with the mouse, then play it again using only Tab and Enter. Every part of it, from the question number to the colour of each button, is drawn from one small object, and Play again can't leave a stale score behind because it builds a fresh one.

The plan has three files, each with one job:

game.js never touches the page, so you can test it in Node. main.js is the only file that knows about HTML.

#Step 1: Questions are data

A question is an object with a prompt, a list of choices, the index of the right choice, and a short explanation. Adding a question means adding an object, not writing new code.

answer counts from 0, which is easy to get wrong when you're typing questions late at night. A quiz that marks the right answer wrong is worse than one that doesn't start, so the game checks the data first and throws a clear error for the first problem it finds.

The message names the question and says what's wrong with it, so whoever wrote the questions can fix it in seconds. checkQuestions goes in game.js.

#Step 2: The whole game is one object and four functions

What does the game need to know at any moment? Which screen it's on, which question, the score, which choice was picked, and the best score. That's the entire state:

screen is one of "start", "question", "feedback" (an answer was picked), or "done". Each update function takes the current state and returns a new one. None of them touches the page.

startGame builds on createGame, so a new game always starts from the same clean values; only best carries over. The first line of pickAnswer and nextQuestion is a guard: a second click on an answer can't add another point, because by then the screen is "feedback".

Because these are plain functions, you can play a whole game in Node. The export keywords are left off here so it runs as one file.

The double click didn't count twice, the best score went from 0 to 1, and playing again reset the score but kept the best. You've tested the hardest part of the game without opening a browser.

#Step 3: render() draws whichever screen the state says

Now the page. index.html contains almost nothing, because render() builds each screen from scratch:

The start of main.js imports the other two files and sets up the state. The helper el creates an element with text and attributes in one line.

Each screen gets a function that returns a list of elements, and render() picks one:

The question and feedback screens share renderQuestion(), because feedback is the same question with the answer revealed. When state.screen is "feedback", it disables the choices, adds a ✓ to the right answer and a ✗ with "(your answer)" to a wrong pick, and adds the explanation and a Next button. Marking answers with symbols and words as well as green and red means the quiz still works for someone who can't tell those colours apart. The full function is in the finished main.js below.

#Step 4: One click listener for every button

render() throws away the old buttons and makes new ones every time, so a listener attached to a button would be thrown away with it. Instead, listen once on #app, which never changes, and look at what was clicked. Each button carries a data-action attribute saying what it's for.

This is the event delegation you met in Module 4. Clicks bubble up from the button to its parents, and closest("button[data-action]") finds the button even if the click landed on text inside it. Look at the shape of the handler: every branch is "replace state with what an update function returns", followed by a single render(). There's nowhere for a second copy of the score to hide.

#Step 5: Put the keyboard focus somewhere useful

When render() replaces the buttons, the button that had focus disappears, and focus falls back to the top of the page. A keyboard user would have to Tab all the way back down after every answer. So each screen marks one element with data-focus, and the last line of render() focuses it: the Start button, the first choice, the Next button, or Play again.

The Next button also has aria-describedby="why", pointing at the explanation paragraph. When focus lands on it, a screen reader reads the button's name and then the explanation, so "Correct!" or "Not quite" is heard straight away.

#Step 6: Save the best score, safely

The best score is a single number, so it's stored as a string and read back with Number. Both functions use try/catch, because storage can be blocked, and a quiz should still be playable without it. Put this code near the top of main.js, above let state, because loadBest() runs as soon as the state is created.

Here || is the right tool. Number(null) is 0 and Number("oops") is NaN, and NaN || 0 turns damaged data into 0. A real saved 0 also becomes 0, which is the same thing.

Now break it on purpose. In questions.js, change one answer to 7 and save. Instead of a quiz that quietly marks the right answer wrong, you get "This quiz can't start" with the exact question to fix. Change it back.

#The finished main.js

Put checkQuestions from Step 1 and the four functions from Step 2 in game.js (each with export in front), the questions in questions.js, the CSS from the preview in style.css, and this in main.js. Open index.html with Live Server, since modules don't load from a double-clicked file.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the click listener go on #app instead of on each button?

  • They can. The problem is that these buttons don't last long enough to keep one.

  • Listeners on the old buttons would be thrown away with them. A single listener on #app catches every click as it bubbles up.

  • Speed is the same. Delegation is about elements that come and go.

Show answer

B. Listeners on the old buttons would be thrown away with them. A single listener on #app catches every click as it bubbles up.

2Why do pickAnswer and nextQuestion return a new object instead of changing the page?

  • They only turn one state into another. render() is the only code that touches the page, so the page always matches state.

  • Modules can do anything a normal script can. Keeping game.js page-free is a design choice.

  • Making new objects uses slightly more memory, not less. The benefit is clarity and testability.

Show answer

A. They only turn one state into another. render() is the only code that touches the page, so the page always matches state.

3You change a question's answer to 7, but it only has three choices. What happens?

  • That's what would happen without checkQuestions, which is exactly why it's there.

  • checkQuestions throws a normal Error, which is caught before anything renders.

  • The try/catch around checkQuestions stores the message in problem, and render() shows it instead of a broken game.

Show answer

C. The try/catch around checkQuestions stores the message in problem, and render() shows it instead of a broken game.

Key takeaways

  • Data (questions.js), logic (game.js), and the page (main.js) each get their own module.
  • The game state is one small object. Update functions take a state and return a new one, and they never touch the page.
  • Pure logic can be tested in Node, a whole playthrough in a few lines.
  • render() rebuilds the current screen from state, so a single click listener on a parent that never changes handles every button.
  • Moving focus after each render, and marking answers with words as well as colours, keeps the quiz usable for everyone.
  • Check data on startup and show a clear error screen rather than a quietly broken app.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Load the questions with fetch. Move them to questions.json and load it with await fetch("./questions.json"), adding a loading screen and an error screen to state.screen.
  • Shuffle. Shuffle the questions in startGame so each game is in a different order (look up the Fisher-Yates shuffle).
  • A timer per question. Give each question 15 seconds with the endAt pattern from the pomodoro build; when time runs out, treat it as a wrong answer.
  • Number keys. Let keys 1 to 4 pick an answer. Listen for keydown on document and call the same pickAnswer.
  • Review screen. Save each pick in an answers array in state and show a summary of every question on the results screen.

#Further reading

  • MDN: JavaScript modules (opens in a new tab): named exports, default exports, and how the browser loads module files.
  • MDN: Element.closest() (opens in a new tab): the method that makes event delegation short.
  • MDN: aria-describedby (opens in a new tab): how to connect a control to the text that explains it.

What you'll learn

  • Move state out of the page and into an object that render() draws from.
  • Derive totals instead of storing them, and keep money in whole cents.
  • Write update functions that return new state and throw clear errors for bad input.
  • Load saved data defensively, split code into modules, and give async work a proper error state.

The Node exercises test pure logic, which is where state bugs are easiest to find. The browser ones are previews you can click, or files to run with Live Server.

#Warm-up: spot the problem

Check your understanding

2 questions

1A to-do app keeps a todos array and a separate count variable, adding 1 in the add handler and subtracting 1 in the delete handler. What's the risk?

  • Today, maybe. The day someone adds "clear completed" and forgets count, the number on screen is wrong.

  • A value you can calculate from other state shouldn't be stored. Then it can never disagree.

  • todos.length is always exact.

Show answer

B. A value you can calculate from other state shouldn't be stored. Then it can never disagree.

2What is name after const name = data.profile?.name ?? "Guest"; if data is { profile: { name: "" } }?

  • ?? only steps in for null or undefined. An empty string is a real value, so it's kept.

  • That's what || would give, since "" is falsy.

  • profile exists, so ?. carries on and reads name.

Show answer

A. ?? only steps in for null or undefined. An empty string is a real value, so it's kept.

#Exercise 1: Stop keeping the count in the page

This counter "works", but the page itself is the state: every handler reads the number back out of the text. Now the counter needs to show whether the count is even or odd, and the best count reached so far. Rewrite it with a state object and a render() function, then add both.

Need a hint?

Try the quick way first: put "(even)" inside the same span and watch Number(countEl.textContent) turn into NaN. That's why the page shouldn't be the state. Is "even or odd" a fact you store, or something you work out? What about "best so far"?

Show solution

"Even or odd" is derived from count every time render() runs, so it's never stored. "Best" has to be stored, because once the count drops you can't work out what it used to be. All three buttons go through setCount, so best can't be forgotten by one of them.

#Exercise 2: Work out the cart totals

Write cartSummary(items) for a shop cart. Each item has a priceCents and a qty. Return the number of items, the subtotal, an 8% tax rounded to the nearest cent, and the total, all in cents. An empty cart should give zeros, not NaN. Then print it as money.

Need a hint?

Loop once, adding item.qty to a count and item.priceCents * item.qty to a subtotal. Round the tax with Math.round. Keep everything in whole cents until the last moment, then divide by 100 and use toFixed(2) only to display it.

Show solution

Only items is state. Count, subtotal, tax, and total are all derived, so changing a quantity can't leave a stale total on screen. An empty cart works with no special case, because the loop just never runs.

#Exercise 3: Update functions that say no

Write addTask(state, text) and toggleTask(state, id) for a to-do list whose state is { tasks: [], nextId: 1 }. Both return a new state and leave the old one untouched. addTask trims the text and throws an error for empty text or a duplicate (ignoring capital letters). toggleTask throws if there's no task with that id.

Need a hint?

array.some((t) => …) is true if any item passes the test, which is perfect for the duplicate and "does this id exist" checks. For a new array with one item changed, use map and return { ...t, done: !t.done } for the matching task and t for the rest. Spread ([...state.tasks, task]) adds to a copy instead of pushing onto the original.

Show solution

The nextId counter means ids are never reused, even after tasks are deleted. The error messages are written for people, so the form's submit handler can put error.message straight into a status line.

#Exercise 4: Load settings you can't trust

Saved settings are { volume, theme, nickname } with defaults 50, "light", and "Player". Write loadSettings(text) that takes the saved JSON text and always returns a complete, valid settings object. volume must be a number from 0 to 100, theme must be "light" or "dark", and nickname must be a non-empty string (trimmed). Anything else falls back to its default, one field at a time.

Need a hint?

Parse inside try, and return the defaults if it throws or gives something that isn't an object (JSON.parse("null") is null). Then check each field on its own with typeof or Number.isFinite. A volume of 0 must survive, which rules out saved.volume || 50.

Show solution

Checking each field separately means one bad value (a purple theme) doesn't throw away the good ones (a volume of 0). In the browser, call it as loadSettings(localStorage.getItem("settings")), inside the same try you'd use for any storage access.

#Exercise 5: Split a file into modules

Split this one-file shop page into cart.js (the logic, with no page code) and main.js (everything that touches the page). Then answer three questions: what happens if you forget export on cartTotal, if you write from "./cart" without .js, and if you double-click index.html instead of using Live Server?

Need a hint?

Ask of each function: does it use document? If not, it belongs in cart.js and gets export. The cart variable is state, so it lives in main.js with the code that changes it. Don't forget to change the script tag.

Show solution

The three mistakes:

  1. No export on cartTotal: SyntaxError: The requested module './cart.js' does not provide an export named 'cartTotal', and none of main.js runs, not even the lines before the problem.
  2. "./cart" without .js: the browser asks Live Server for a file literally called cart, gets a 404, and the Console shows a red 404 (Not Found) error for that address. The Network panel shows the failed request too.
  3. Double-clicking the file: the page opens from file://, and the Console reports that the script was "blocked by CORS policy". Modules need a server.

#Exercise 6: Loading, error, and "Try again"

Build a page that loads a class list from a (fake) server. Track the request with a status field in state: "idle", "loading", "error", or "ready". Show a Load button when idle, "Loading…" while loading, the error with a Try again button on failure, and the list when ready. The fake server fails the first time and works the second, so you can see every state.

Need a hint?

Write a load() function that sets status = "loading" and renders, awaits the fake server inside try, and sets "ready" with the data or "error" with the message in catch, rendering again at the end. render() is a set of if branches, one per status. Use one click listener on the container with data-action, as in the quiz game.

Show solution

Because status is a single field, the page can't be "loading" and "showing an error" at the same time, a mix that happens easily when you track isLoading and hasError as separate booleans. The diagram above is the whole design: every arrow is a line in load(), and every circle is a branch in render().

#Challenge: an Undo button

Add Undo to the to-do functions from Exercise 3. Keep a history array of earlier states; every successful update pushes the old state first, and undo() pops the most recent one back. Keep at most 20 entries. Then answer: why is this easy because addTask and toggleTask return new objects instead of changing the old one?

Need a hint?

Write apply(update), which runs update(state) inside try, and only if it succeeds pushes the old state onto history and replaces state. history.slice(-20) keeps the last 20. If an update throws, nothing should be pushed.

Show solution

Each old state is a separate object that nothing else changes, so keeping a reference to it is a perfect snapshot. If the update functions changed state.tasks in place, every entry in history would point at the same array and Undo would bring back the current list. The refused update didn't create a history entry, so Undo never steps back to a state that didn't change.

What you'll learn

  • Know exactly what the capstone app has to do, and where in the course you learned each part.
  • Choose a project idea that fits your time and skill.
  • Write a one-page plan: features, state, saved data, data source, screens, and events.
  • Check an API works from the browser before you build on it.

Here's a good test for a finished app. Someone you've never met opens it on a phone over a slow connection. They use it for a minute, refresh halfway through, and lose their signal for a moment. They still get what they came for, and nothing on the screen ever says undefined.

Your capstone is an app that passes that test. You've built every piece already: a timer that survives a refresh, a profile viewer that handles a 404, a quiz whose state can't disagree with itself. Now you'll put them together in something of your own. The first step happens away from the keyboard, because an hour of planning saves days of rewriting.

#What your app must do

Requirement What it means in practice Where you learned it
Data in arrays and objects The app's information is modelled as data, not scattered through the HTML. Module 2
The page is drawn from state One state object; render() updates the page from it. Modules 3 and 7
Mouse and keyboard events Every action works with a click and with Tab and Enter. Module 4
Validated input Bad input gets a specific message that says how to fix it. Module 4
Saved state The important data survives a refresh, a first visit, and damaged saved data. Module 5
At least one async operation fetch from a public API, or from a JSON file in your own project folder. Module 6
Every state of the data Loading, empty, success, and error each look intentional. Modules 6 and 7
Responsive layout Usable from a 320-pixel-wide phone up to a laptop. Your CSS

A timer is welcome but not required. If your idea needs one, reuse the endAt pattern from the pomodoro build.

#Five project ideas

Each idea has a core you should finish and a stretch goal for later. The stars are a rough guide to how much work it is.

1. Habit tracker (★, a solid first capstone). A list of habits like "read 20 minutes" or "drink water", each with a check box for today and a streak count. Habits and their completed days are saved. The async part: a "suggestions" panel loads ideas from a habits.json file in your project with fetch("./habits.json"), with loading and error states. Stretch: a seven-day grid for each habit drawn with CSS.

2. Quiz show (★★). Grow the quiz from Module 7 into a real game: questions in questions.json, grouped by category, with a 15-second timer per question and the best score saved for each category. Stretch: a review screen that shows every question with your answer and the right one.

3. Dog breed explorer (★★). Fill a drop-down with every breed from https://dog.ceo/api/breeds/list/all, then show a random photo of the chosen breed from https://dog.ceo/api/breed/beagle/images/random (with beagle replaced by the breed). A heart button saves favourite photos, and a Favourites view shows them even offline (the image addresses are saved; the pictures need a connection). Stretch: compare two breeds side by side.

4. Weather dashboard (★★★). Save a list of places with a name, latitude, and longitude, and show the current temperature and wind for each from the free Open-Meteo (opens in a new tab) API, for example https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=40.71&longitude=-74.01&current=temperature_2m,wind_speed_10m. Validate the coordinates (latitude from -90 to 90, longitude from -180 to 180), add a °C/°F switch that's saved (&temperature_unit=fahrenheit), and show "Updated 12 minutes ago" so stale data is obvious. Stretch: an hourly forecast for the next 12 hours.

5. Reading list with book search (★★★). Search the Open Library (opens in a new tab) catalogue with https://openlibrary.org/search.json?q=hatchet&limit=10&fields=title,author_name,first_publish_year,cover_i, add results to your own list, and mark each book as "want to read", "reading", or "finished", with filters. Search-as-you-type needs the debounce from Module 5 and the "latest request wins" fix from Module 6. Stretch: covers from https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/ followed by the cover_i number and -M.jpg.

Your own idea is welcome if it meets every requirement in the table. Run it past the checklist at the end of this lesson first.

📝 Note

All three APIs above are free, need no key, and allow requests from a page on Live Server. Be a polite guest anyway: never send a request on every key press without debouncing, and cache answers you already have. And never put a secret API key in front-end code. Anyone can read your JavaScript in DevTools, so a key in it isn't secret.

#Check the API before you commit to it

Ten minutes now can save you from building on something that won't work. For any API you plan to use:

  1. Open the address in a browser tab. You should see JSON. Save one real response in your notes; you'll need the exact field names.
  2. Call it from your page. In a script.js served by Live Server, fetch it and console.log the result. If the Console says the request was blocked by CORS policy, that API doesn't allow requests from other websites' pages, and no JavaScript on your side can fix it. Pick another one.
  3. Try a bad request. Misspell a breed or search for nonsense. Note the status code and what the body looks like, because your error state will need it.
  4. Read the limits. Look for "rate limit" in the docs, and plan for what your app shows when you hit it.

If you choose a local JSON file instead, write it by hand with five to ten realistic entries, and include one entry with a missing field so you can test your defensive code.

#Write a one-page plan

Copy this template into a file called plan.txt in your project folder and fill in every line. Short answers are fine; blank ones aren't.

The most important lines are STATE and SAVED. If you can write the state object now, with real example values, you understand your app. If you can't, you're not ready to code it yet, and that's useful to know now rather than halfway through the build.

#A worked example: the habit tracker

Here's the plan's heart for idea 1, written as the actual starting state:

Derived, not stored: whether a habit is done today (doneDays includes today's date key), each habit's streak (the currentStreak function from the Module 5 challenge), and the count of habits done today. Saved: habits and nextId, under the key habit-tracker, loaded with the defensive pattern from Module 7. suggestions isn't saved, because it can be loaded again.

Then the screens. Writing down all four states for every piece of data is the step most people skip, and it's where most "it works on my machine" bugs come from.

Part of the page Loading Empty Success Error
Habit list (none; it's local) "No habits yet. Add your first one above." The list, with streaks Saved data damaged: start fresh and say so once
Suggestions panel "Loading ideas…" "No suggestions right now." Clickable idea chips "Couldn't load ideas." plus a Try again button
New habit form The habit appears in the list "Give the habit a name" or "You already track that"

And the shape of the code, which next lesson's starter follows:

#Cut it down to something you can finish

Look at your MUST HAVE list and be honest. A small app that handles every case beats a big one that breaks when the network is slow. A good rule: if your must-have list has more than five items, move the last ones to NICE TO HAVE. You can always add them after the rubric is satisfied.

Next lesson splits the build into six milestones, each ending with something that works. Estimate how long each will take you, then add half again. Things always take longer than planned, and that's normal, not a sign you're doing it wrong.

Key takeaways

  • The capstone must model data, render from one state object, handle mouse and keyboard, validate input, save state, do at least one async operation, show loading, empty, success, and error states, and work on a phone.
  • Choose an idea by honest size. A finished ★ app beats an unfinished ★★★ one.
  • Check an API in a browser tab and from a Live Server page (watch for CORS errors) before you build on it.
  • Write the state object with real example values before writing any other code.
  • List all four data states for every part of the page.

#Before you move on

Your plan is ready when you can answer yes to all of these:

  • The STATE section is a real object with example values.
  • You know which fields are saved, and under what key.
  • You've seen a real response from your data source, and a real error response.
  • Every screen has its loading, empty, success, and error states written down.
  • Your must-have list has five items or fewer.

#Further reading

  • Open-Meteo API docs (opens in a new tab): an interactive page that builds the forecast URL for you, a quick way to explore the data.
  • Open Library Search API (opens in a new tab): search fields, paging, and how to ask for only the fields you need.
  • Dog CEO API (opens in a new tab): every endpoint for breeds, sub-breeds, and random images.

m8-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Set up a project from a starter that already handles saving, loading, errors, and focus.
  • Build in milestones that each end with something that works.
  • Know when a milestone is done, using a concrete checklist for each.
  • Debug with the Console, breakpoints, console.table, and the Network and Application panels.

Most unfinished projects fail the same way: everything is half-built and nothing works. The cure is to build in milestones. Each one adds one layer, ends with an app that runs, and has a checklist that says when you're done. If you run out of time at milestone 4, you still have a working app that saves its data, not a pile of pieces.

#The starter

The starter is a small, complete app: a list you can add to, tick off, and remove from, that saves itself and loads "ideas" from a JSON file. It's deliberately plain, so you can turn it into any of the five project ideas (or your own) by changing the data and the screens. Every place you're expected to change is marked CHANGE.

Make the folders and files, and paste in the code below. Then right-click index.html, choose Open with Live Server, and check it runs before you change anything.

storage.js is the Module 5 pattern, made unbreakable: loadSaved returns the saved value or null, and save returns false instead of throwing. Put a version in the key (-v1) so that if you change the shape of your saved data later, you can switch to -v2 and start clean.

api.js is the getJSON helper from the GitHub viewer, with the timeout from the Module 6 challenge built in, plus one function that turns any error into a sentence.

state.js holds every rule of the app, and none of it touches the page. Notice two different ways of saying no. Bad input is expected, so addItem returns a state with a formError message to show. Damaged saved data is cleaned up by createInitialState, which keeps only items with the right shape. Errors are thrown only for things that really shouldn't happen, and those are caught in main.js.

render.js builds the page from state, with an empty message for an empty list and a separate branch for each of the four states of the ideas panel.

main.js connects everything. All changes go through update(), which saves, redraws, and then puts keyboard focus back on the same control. Without that last part, ticking a box with the Space bar would redraw the list and throw focus back to the top of the page.

Try it: add an item, tick it, refresh. Add the same item twice. Click an idea. Then open DevTools and work through the milestones below, turning the starter into your app.

#Milestone 1: The layout, on a phone first

Change index.html and style.css to match your plan's screens, with a few hard-coded example entries so you can see the design. No JavaScript changes yet. Then open DevTools, click Toggle device toolbar, leave Dimensions on Responsive, and type 320 into the width box.

Done when:

  • Nothing scrolls sideways at 320 pixels wide, and the layout still looks deliberate at 1,200.
  • Every input has a visible label, and every button says what it does.
  • Pressing Tab moves through the controls in the same order you read them.

#Milestone 2: State and render(), with fake data

Delete the hard-coded entries from the HTML. Change createInitialState so it starts with two or three example items in your app's shape (a habit with doneDays, a city with latitude, a book with status), and change render.js to draw them.

Done when:

  • Editing the example data in state.js changes the page, and nothing in render.js reads values back from the page.
  • Values you can calculate (counts, streaks, totals) are calculated in render, not stored.
  • console.table(state.items) in update() shows exactly what you expect.

#Milestone 3: Events and validation

Add the update functions your EVENTS list needs (each one in state.js, each returning a new state) and connect them with data-action buttons. Write a validation message for every way input can be wrong, and test each one in Node before wiring it to the page, the way you tested the quiz.

Done when:

  • Every action works with the mouse and with Tab, Enter, and Space.
  • Every bad input (empty, too long, duplicate, out of range) shows a specific message, and the message disappears when the person starts fixing it.
  • Clicking any button twice quickly never breaks anything.

#Milestone 4: Save and restore

Change the storage key, and change toSave and createInitialState so they save and restore your app's real data, keeping only well-formed entries.

Done when:

  • A refresh keeps everything the person would be upset to lose.
  • In Application › Storage, clicking Clear site data and refreshing gives a clean first-visit screen with no errors.
  • Editing your saved value in Local storage to {oops and refreshing starts fresh instead of crashing.

#Milestone 5: Load data, and show all four states

Point getJSON at your real API or JSON file and adapt ideasLoaded (rename it for your app) to clean up the response. Before testing with the network, check that each state looks intentional. A quick way is a state switcher: render the same function with an example state for each case and flip between them. Here it is for the starter's ideas panel; use the menu to see each state.

This works because renderIdeas only looks at its argument. Then test the real thing in the Network panel.

Done when:

  • With throttling on Slow 4G, you can read the loading message.
  • With Offline, you get your error message, and Try again works once you go back to No throttling.
  • A response with no results (an empty search, or [] in your JSON file) shows the empty state, not a blank space.
  • If you search as the person types, the latest request always wins (Module 6, Exercise 6).

#Milestone 6: Polish

Now make it feel finished. Work through the test plan in the next lesson and fix what it finds. Typical polish: a page title that names your app, messages that say what to do next, visible focus on every control, alt text for every image that carries information, and removing leftover console.log and console.table lines.

Done when: every row of the next lesson's test plan passes.

#When you get stuck

Use the routine from Module 1 (read the error, check the line, add a log), and add these tools:

  • Click the file name in a Console error (like render.js:27) to jump to the exact line in the Sources panel.
  • Set a breakpoint by clicking a line number in Sources, or write debugger; in your code. When execution stops there, hover over any variable to see its value, and use Step over to run one line at a time.
  • console.table(state.items) prints an array of objects as a table, which makes a wrong field obvious.
  • Network › Fetch/XHR shows every request, its status, and the exact response, so you can tell "my code is wrong" from "the server said no".
  • Application › Local storage shows what you actually saved, which is often not what you think you saved.

💡 Tip

At the end of each milestone, copy the whole project folder (for example to capstone-m3). If milestone 4 goes badly wrong, you can go back to a version that worked in seconds. If you already know Git, commit at the end of every milestone instead.

Key takeaways

  • Build in layers: layout, state and render, events, storage, async data, polish. Each layer ends with an app that runs.
  • Keep every rule in state.js as a pure function, and test it in Node before wiring it up.
  • Route every change through one update() that saves, renders, and restores focus.
  • Look at each state on purpose (a state switcher makes it quick), then prove it with throttling and Offline.
  • Save a copy at every milestone, and debug with breakpoints instead of guesswork.

#Further reading

What you'll learn

  • Write quick automated checks for the rules in state.js.
  • Run a test plan that covers the situations real people hit, using DevTools to fake each one.
  • Polish the details that make an app feel finished.
  • Write a README, give a three-minute demo, and assess your work against the rubric.

Your app works: on your computer, with your data, when you click things in the order you expect. Testing is finding out what happens the rest of the time. The good news is that you designed for most of it already. Now you prove it.

#Check the rules automatically

The rules of your app live in state.js as pure functions, so you can check them in Node in a few seconds, as often as you like. You don't need a testing library: a check function that compares what you got with what you expected is enough. Here it is testing the starter's rules. The functions are copied in without export so the file runs on its own.

Write one check for every rule in your own state.js, especially the edge cases from your plan: empty input, a duplicate, a value out of range, damaged saved data, a response with missing fields. Run the file after every change. When a check fails, the name tells you which rule broke before you've even opened the browser.

#The test plan

Copy this table into plan.txt and add a Result column. Run every row on your finished app, write pass or fail, and fix each fail before moving on. Run the whole plan again after the fixes, because fixes break things too.

# Situation How to make it happen It passes when
1 First visit Application › Storage › Clear site data, then refresh A clean, friendly empty state; no red errors in the Console
2 Refresh in the middle Do half the main task, then refresh Everything the person would mind losing is still there
3 Damaged saved data In Local storage, double-click your value, type {oops, refresh The app starts fresh instead of crashing
4 Slow network Network throttling: Slow 4G The loading state is visible, and clicking twice doesn't send duplicates
5 No network Throttling: Offline A clear error message with a way to try again, which works once back online
6 Nothing found Search for nonsense, or make your JSON file [] An empty state that suggests what to do next
7 Server says no Misspell the API path in getJSON for a moment A specific message, not a crash or a blank space
8 Bad input Try empty, very long, duplicate, and out-of-range values A specific message for each, and nothing bad is saved
9 Impatient clicks Click every button five times, fast No duplicates, no errors, no stuck loading message
10 Keyboard only Put the mouse away; use Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space The whole main task works; focus is always visible and never jumps to the top
11 Small screen Toggle device toolbar, width 320 No sideways scrolling; buttons are easy to tap
12 Zoomed in Zoom the page to 200% (Ctrl and +, or Cmd and + on a Mac) Everything is still readable and usable
13 Accessibility basics Run a Lighthouse report with Accessibility ticked Labels, alt text, contrast, and names pass; fix anything flagged
14 Clean Console Watch the Console during all of the above No red errors, and no leftover debugging logs

Rows 3, 5, and 10 find the most bugs. They're also the ones most people skip.

#Polish: the details people notice

Polish is mostly words and focus. Go through this list once your test plan passes:

  • Empty states give a next step. "No habits yet. Add your first one above." beats a blank box.
  • Error messages say what happened and what to do: "Couldn't reach the weather service. Check your connection and try again."
  • Buttons describe their result. "Add habit" and "Save city", not "Submit" and "OK".
  • Focus is always visible (keep :focus-visible styles) and always lands somewhere sensible after an action.
  • Status messages are announced. Loading, saved, and error messages go in an aria-live="polite" element that exists from the start.
  • Colour is never the only signal. Pair red and green with words or symbols.
  • Motion is optional. If you added animations, turn them off for people who've asked their system for less motion with @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce).
  • The tab title names the app, and a timer or count can go in it too.

#Write a README

A README is the first thing anyone reads about your project, including future you. Save this as README.md in your project folder and fill it in. The # lines are headings in Markdown, which GitHub displays nicely.

The "How it handles problems" section is where your app stands out. Most beginner projects don't have one, because most beginner projects don't handle problems.

#Present it in three minutes

Practise this once out loud with a timer. Three minutes goes quickly.

  1. The problem (20 seconds). Who is it for, and what do they get done?
  2. The main task, live (60 seconds). Do the thing the app is for, start to finish.
  3. Prove it's sturdy (40 seconds). Refresh and show nothing was lost. Switch the Network panel to Offline and show the error and the retry. Type something invalid and show the message.
  4. Behind the scenes (40 seconds). Show your state object, and tell the story of one bug: what went wrong, how you found it, how you fixed it.
  5. What's next (20 seconds). The first thing on your NICE TO HAVE list.

#Put it online (optional)

GitHub Pages hosts static sites like yours for free. You'll need a GitHub account (GitHub requires users to be at least 13). Create a public repository and upload your project files with Add file › Upload files, keeping index.html at the top level. Then go to the repository's Settings › Pages, and under Build and deployment set Source to Deploy from a branch, choose your main branch and the root folder, and click Save. After a minute or two your app is live at https://your-username.github.io/repository-name/.

Everything on GitHub Pages is public, so check your files for anything personal before you upload. Each visitor's localStorage is their own, so their data stays in their browser.

#The rubric

Score your own app honestly before anyone else does. Each criterion has full marks and partial marks; anything less than partial scores zero for that row.

Criterion Points Full marks Partial marks (about half)
Main task works 20 Every must-have feature works from start to finish The main task works with rough edges, or one must-have is missing
State and code organisation 15 One state object; render() draws from it; rules live in pure functions in their own module State is mostly in one place, but some values are read from or stored in the page
Saved data 10 Survives refresh; first visit and damaged data both handled Saves and restores, but fails test 1 or test 3
Async data and its states 15 Loading, empty, success, and error all look intentional, and retry works Success plus one or two of the other states
Validation and messages 10 Every bad input gets a specific message that says how to fix it Some validation, or only generic messages
Accessibility and layout 15 Keyboard-only use works with visible focus; labels and alt text; usable at 320 px and 200% zoom Mostly usable, with a few problem controls or sizes
Testing 10 Node checks for the rules, and the full test plan with results A few checks, or a partly completed plan
README and demo 5 The README covers running it and handling problems; the demo fits three minutes One of the two is missing or incomplete

A total of 85 or more is excellent work, 70 to 84 is solid, and below 70 means there's a row or two worth another evening.

#Look back, then look ahead

Answer these in a few sentences each. They're for you, and they make the best material for your presentation:

  1. Which bug took longest to find, and what finally revealed it?
  2. Where did keeping state in one object save you trouble? Where did it feel awkward?
  3. What would you design differently if you started again tomorrow?
  4. Which test plan row found the most problems?

You now know the ideas that every front-end framework is built on: state, a render step, events that update state, async data with loading and error states, and modules. When you meet a framework such as React, Svelte, or Vue, you'll recognise render() and the state object straight away; the framework mostly does the redrawing for you. Good next steps are TypeScript (JavaScript with types, which catches many bugs before you run the code), a testing tool that grows out of your check function, and building a small back end of your own, so the API your app talks to is one you wrote.

#Further reading

  • W3C: Easy checks for web accessibility (opens in a new tab): a first review you can do in 20 minutes, from page titles to keyboard access.
  • GitHub Docs: Creating a GitHub Pages site (opens in a new tab): the official steps, with screenshots of every setting.
  • MDN: Learn web development (opens in a new tab): free, well-organised next steps in HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and accessibility.
